#5567. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

EXTRA: What Compass’ leadership ban signals for agents and associations

#5565. AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

“Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”

Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.)

Axelera’s Europa chip has been shipping since September. Ahead of SC26, the company unveiled Titania, a third-generation architecture that scales the design up to a 400-watt chip. The resulting six-kilowatt server is built to perform like leading data center GPUs while fitting into the existing 20- to 30-kilowatt air-cooled racks of an ordinary enterprise data center, Botija explained.

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”

For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the company’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.”

#5564. CobbleStone® Announces December 3rd CLE Webinar on Responsible AI Use in Corporate and In-House Legal Practice

AI ethics webinar helps legal professionals understand responsible AI use while earning CLE credit.

PRINCETON, N.J., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CobbleStone Software, a recognized leader in contract lifecycle management (CLM) and contract artificial intelligence, announced its upcoming CLE webinar, "AI & Ethics: Responsible AI Use in Corporate and In-House Legal Practice," scheduled for December 3, 2026, from 2:00 PM to 3:00 PM ET. The complimentary educational event will provide legal professionals with practical guidance on the ethical implications of responsible AI adoption, including privilege and waiver.

The webinar will be presented by a leading AI attorney and will offer a plain-English explanation of how artificial intelligence technologies function, helping attendees better understand the ethical and professional responsibility challenges associated with AI use by lawyers. Participants will also gain insight into how courts are addressing AI-related privilege and waiver issues and receive actionable recommendations for minimizing ethical risks when leveraging AI tools in legal environments.

Attendees will receive a resource guide featuring key bar association guidance and notable judicial decisions related to AI ethics, attorney-client privilege, and more. Live attendees may also qualify for CLE credit, subject to their state's specific accreditation requirements. Credits have been approved or are pending in numerous jurisdictions across the United States.

Legal professionals today face increasing pressure to adopt AI technologies while maintaining compliance with ethical obligations and professional standards. Understanding how courts, regulators, and bar associations view AI-assisted legal work is becoming increasingly important as organizations evaluate new technologies and workflows. The webinar is designed to address these challenges by providing practical, current guidance tailored to attorneys working in corporate legal departments, law firms, and related legal functions.

Register for the complimentary CLE webinar today to reserve your spot and learn how to navigate emerging AI ethics considerations with greater confidence.

"Artificial intelligence presents tremendous opportunities for legal professionals. It also raises important ethical questions that cannot be ignored," said Bradford Jones, VP of Sales & Marketing at CobbleStone Software.

"This webinar is designed to help attorneys understand AI in terms of what ethical considerations they should be aware of and how they can responsibly use these technologies while protecting client interests and maintaining professional standards."

#5563. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5562. Broker Action Coalition pushes for QM change on compensation cap

The Broker Action Coalition wants lender-paid broker compensation excluded from QM points and fees, aligning with retail LO pay. BAC says the current treatment harms small-balance and rural loans, citing 2026 wholesale data and prior CFPB findings.  AI Summary

The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.

In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.

Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026. Smaller loans are subject to graduated percentage and dollar limits.

Currently, compensation paid by a wholesale lender to an independent mortgage broker counts toward that limit, while compensation paid by a retail lender to its own employee loan officer is excluded.

The coalition argues that both types of compensation are often funded through the interest rate and are indistinguishable from the borrower’s perspective. The difference can leave brokers with less room to cover other fees that count toward the cap, potentially causing otherwise qualifying loans to exceed the limit while losing QM status and its associated liability protections.

The disparity is particularly pronounced on smaller loans, where the dollar limits leave less room for additional charges. The coalition said small-balance and rural loans are particularly vulnerable because fixed-dollar charges consume a larger share of the available cap.

The white paper also points to a decline in small-dollar mortgage lending. The share of home purchase loans under $70,000 fell from more than 11% in 2011 to less than 4% in 2020, citing research from Pew Charitable Trusts, the Urban Institute and the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

In rural and lower-cost markets, the group argues, the restrictions can make it harder for brokers to compete for loans that are already less financially attractive to originate.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau‘s 2013 rulemaking established the distinction between employee and broker compensation. At the time, the bureau said including broker compensation in the calculation could help reduce the risk of mortgage brokers steering borrowers toward more expensive transactions.

The coalition acknowledges that consumer protection concern but argues that subsequent regulations addressing loan originator compensation and steering have made the points-and-fees restriction a less targeted way to address the issue.

Specifically, the group points to existing rules that prohibit loan originator compensation from varying based on a loan’s interest rate or other terms, as well as a separate prohibition on steering borrowers toward transactions that provide greater compensation.

The proposed reform would take two approaches: The primary proposal is a statutory amendment to the Truth in Lending Act that would exclude rate-funded creditor-to-broker compensation from the points-and-fees definition when it is paid under a compliant loan originator compensation agreement.

The parallel regulatory proposal would ask the CFPB to amend Regulation Z to create the same exclusion.

“The proposed reform would remove an inequitable regulatory constraint without changing the competitive forces that influence compensation today,” the paper reads. “While individual brokerages may adjust their compensation arrangements, there is little evidence to suggest that the reform would materially diminish the wholesale channel‘s overall pricing competitiveness.”

Under the proposed language, the exclusion would apply only when compensation is funded through the interest rate, is not paid directly by the borrower or financed into the loan amount, and is established through a standing agreement between the creditor and broker that does not vary based on individual loan terms.

The coalition said the proposed requirements would prevent brokers from adjusting compensation on individual loans to circumvent the cap. The change would leave the 3% limit and existing compensation and anti-steering rules intact, with borrower-paid compensation and other fees still subject to the cap.

Data from two wholesale lenders representing $13.4 billion in combined 2026 production showed that loans with 2.75% broker compensation accounted for 14.53% of units and 12.41% of volume. BAC said the figures indicate most brokered loans close with lower compensation.

The group also argued that the CFPB has authority under the Truth in Lending Act to make the change to preserve access to affordable mortgage credit. It cited the bureau’s 2019 assessment of the Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage rule, which documented fee waivers and other challenges affecting smaller brokered loans.

#5560. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress said the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the company held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

For information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

One of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he said the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued new export controls this week, which the company “still has some time to study.”

Huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

For IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The new Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

With demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress said. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”

Those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress said the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

The lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain important, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She said Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”

Two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still plans to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

The flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

My advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

The demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress said agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

The CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive new spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress said, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how quickly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, plan CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip company, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

The next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:

Matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves quickly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management company. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the company can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

This call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current plans and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5559. Senate committee advances Matt Jones’ nomination as FHA commissioner

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs voted 13-11 to advance Matt Jones’ nomination as HUD assistant secretary for housing and FHA commissioner, sending it to the full Senate.  AI Summary

Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley, who has been serving in the role on an acting basis.

Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an important role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.”

Jones currently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at Amerifirst Home Mortgage, and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees.The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.”

“We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration‘s disastrous economic policies,” Warren said. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA currently insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages.

The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers.

Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner, including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure.

MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.”

“We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit said.

#5558. Global HVAC Equipment Market to Reach $383.6 Billion by 2031 as AI, Decarbonisation and Smart Cooling Reshape Industry, Finds Frost & Sullivan

New Frost Radarâ¢ analysis profiles 10 leading HVAC equipment companies and highlights emerging growth opportunities in data centre cooling, building electrification and intelligent lifecycle services

LONDON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The global heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment market is projected to reach $383.6 billion by 2031, expanding at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.0% from 2025, according to Frost & Sullivan's latest Frost Radarâ¢: HVAC Equipment, 2026 analysis.

The HVAC industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation as tightening energy-efficiency regulations, decarbonisation commitments and advances in artificial intelligence (AI) accelerate the transition towards intelligent, connected and sustainable climate solutions. The integration of Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors, AI-driven predictive analytics and cloud-based platforms is enabling real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance and energy optimisation, helping building owners and operators improve equipment reliability, reduce lifecycle costs and unlock new opportunities for digitally enabled services.

At the same time, decarbonisation and building electrification are emerging as powerful catalysts for industry growth. Governments worldwide are introducing stricter energy-efficiency standards and environmental regulations, accelerating demand for high-efficiency heat pumps, low-global-warming-potential (GWP) refrigerants and sustainable climate technologies. The transition towards greener buildings and net-zero infrastructure is increasingly influencing product development, investment priorities and procurement decisions across the HVAC value chain.

Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing HVAC equipment market, driven by urbanisation and infrastructure development. In Europe and North America, demand is fuelled primarily by equipment replacement and decarbonisation initiatives, while the Middle East is seeing strong growth in energy-efficient cooling and district cooling infrastructure. Latin America remains an emerging market with more moderate growth prospects.

Frost Radarâ¢ Profiles Leading HVAC Equipment Companies

Against this evolving market backdrop, Frost & Sullivan independently evaluated 25 qualified global HVAC industry participants, selecting 10 companies for benchmarking through its proprietary Frost Radarâ¢ methodology, which assesses innovation capabilities alongside growth performance.

The companies profiled in the Frost Radarâ¢: HVAC Equipment, 2026 analysis are Bosch, Carrier, Daikin Industries, Johnson Controls, LG Electronics, Midea Group, Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, Panasonic Corporation, Samsung Electronics and Trane Technologies.

Frost & Sullivan identifies significant growth opportunities in next-generation data centre cooling, building electrification and connected HVAC services. The expansion of AI infrastructure is driving demand for advanced thermal management solutions, while decarbonisation initiatives are accelerating the adoption of high-efficiency heat pumps and retrofit-compatible technologies. Meanwhile, IoT connectivity, AI-powered diagnostics and predictive maintenance are enabling manufacturers to improve equipment performance, reduce operating costs and transition towards service-led business models that generate recurring revenue and strengthen customer relationships.

"The HVAC industry is moving beyond traditional equipment manufacturing towards a more intelligent, connected and service-driven ecosystem," said Jonathan Robinson, Practice Area Leader, Energy & Buildings, at Frost & Sullivan. "The convergence of AI, decarbonisation and increasingly sophisticated cooling requirements is creating significant opportunities for manufacturers to rethink how they deliver value. Companies that successfully combine energy-efficient technologies with digital intelligence and lifecycle services will be best positioned to capture the next wave of growth."

#5557. Planning to Join the ANT IPO? Binance Opens $500M Tokenized Anthropic Share Sale

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Planning to join Anthropic’s ANT IPO? Binance is giving crypto investors another way to gain exposure to one of the biggest technology listings of 2026. Binance Wallet has opened an eight-hour subscription campaign for Anthropic tokenized stocks through its xStocks partnership. The offering carries a $500 million USDC subscription cap, with indicative prices ranging from $70 to $78 per token.

The campaign opened on November 18 at 06:00 UTC and closes at 14:00 UTC. Eligible participants can apply through Binance Wallet using USDC, with a minimum subscription of 100 USDC. Successful applicants will receive tokenized Anthropic exposure following the allocation process.

The ANT IPO campaign uses an allocation system based on Binance Alpha Points. Users with more than zero Alpha Points receive a subscription quota of $20,000. Higher balances unlock substantially larger limits. Users holding more than 40 points qualify for $100,000, while those exceeding 100 points receive $200,000.

The highest tier requires more than 200 Alpha Points and unlocks a $500,000 subscription quota. Binance also offers an additional $50,000 quota to eligible users holding its Trenchers Badge.

These figures are the maximum subscription limits, not guaranteed allocations. The campaign uses an oversubscription model, meaning successful applicants could receive full or partial allocations.

Participants must commit USDC through a non-custodial smart contract. Unused funds will return to their Binance Wallet after allocation calculations finish. The subscription also carries a 5% partner service fee charged by xStocks. Binance Wallet does not charge an additional participation fee.

Binance has set an indicative subscription price between $70 and $78 per token. This matches Anthropic’s proposed IPO pricing range in its registration filing. Anthropic plans to offer 825 million Class A shares under the proposed listing. The company has applied to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

At the upper end of its proposed price range, the offering implies a valuation of approximately $1.41 trillion. At $70 per share, the implied valuation falls to $1.26 trillion.

The final offering price will depend on demand, valuation conditions, and arrangements between the issuer and underwriters.

The distribution process begins after the application window closes. Successful participants will receive their tokenized exposure after the underlying issuance is completed.

Investors who missed the Anthropic IPO window still have another crypto launch approaching. Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is heading toward its November 26 launch, with its presale already attracting more than $33.2 million.

The token currently sells for just $0.0136, putting it just below its indicated $0.0137 initial listing price. Its staged presale structure increases prices as allocations advance, giving earlier participants access before subsequent price steps. There is also no individual purchase maximum listed, leaving room for larger allocations.

Staking adds another incentive, with rewards offered at 35% APY. That gives early holders an opportunity to accumulate additional HYPER while the project prepares its token launch.

Bitcoin Hyper is building a Bitcoin Layer 2 using Solana Virtual Machine technology. The goal is to combine Bitcoin’s liquidity with Solana-style transaction speed, opening the door to faster BTC transfers, decentralized applications, and on-chain finance.

The timing could prove interesting. Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO is bringing fresh attention to alternative investment opportunities, while Bitcoin Hyper approaches its November 26 milestone. If crypto sentiment recovers alongside renewed institutional interest, HYPER enters the launch window with a $33 million fundraising milestone, an established presale community, and staking incentives already in place.

With the November 26 launch approaching, the remaining presale window is becoming increasingly important for investors watching the next wave of Bitcoin ecosystem projects.

#5556. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

Enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating new requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

“They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane said. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”

Vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the company has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane said Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always said that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

That approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

The next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create new revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane said the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

The goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming important as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

The growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

An AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane said.

CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

Another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

This creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

For organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

Cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

The distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

“If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he said.

That approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

For enterprises, this is an important architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Inference costs can increase quickly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

Cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

He described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

The broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

That moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

Cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

Cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

He also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane said, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain important, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

That creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

As Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

#5555. Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028

Five housing and mortgage trade groups urged FHFA to delay a planned condo reserve requirement increase from 10% to 15% until Jan. 4, 2028. They cited budget cycle constraints, unclear implementation details and potential GSE financing disruptions.  AI Summary

Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions.

In a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte, the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028.

The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income.

The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute, Community Association Roundtable, Community Home Lenders of America (CHLA), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers (NAMB).

The groups said they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change.

Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3.

“Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options,” the groups wrote.

The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that “the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability.”

First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices.

The groups also said questions remain about how the new requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements.

Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to update their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews.

Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values.

The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more “modest-income” homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available.

Lastly, the coalition said higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees.

Fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners’ costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments.

As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding.

“We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives,” the letter said.

#5553. Frost & Sullivan Forecasts Global Cloud Security Market to Reach $26.8 Billion by 2031 as AI and Unified Security Platforms Drive Growth

New research highlights how runtime protection, AI security and managed services are transforming cloud security, creating significant opportunities for technology providers and enterprises

LONDON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The global cloud security market is poised for transformational growth, with revenues projected to increase from $8.4 billion in 2025 to $26.8 billion by 2031, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 21.4%, according to new research from Frost & Sullivan.

The company's latest analysis, Total Cloud Security Market, Global, 2025â2031, reveals how the convergence of cloud-native technologies, AI-driven workloads and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats is accelerating demand for integrated security platforms capable of protecting complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments.

As enterprises move beyond traditional cloud security tools focused on visibility, configuration management and vulnerability detection, attention is shifting towards extended cloud security (XCS) platforms that unify protection across applications, infrastructure, workloads, identities, data and AI systems.

Frost & Sullivan identifies three particularly promising areas for commercial development.

Runtime-informed cloud security operations are gaining momentum as enterprises seek to move beyond identifying vulnerabilities towards understanding which threats pose genuine risks in production environments. This is driving demand for solutions that combine real-time threat detection, exploitability analysis, contextual risk prioritisation and coordinated remediation.

Meanwhile, the proliferation of generative AI applications, autonomous agents and AI-powered workloads is expanding the cloud attack surface, creating opportunities for AI security capabilities that integrate model protection, sensitive data security, identity governance and AI runtime monitoring into existing cloud security platforms.

Growing operational complexity and shortages of specialist cybersecurity talent are also fuelling demand for managed cloud security services. Managed security providers, systems integrators and cloud partners are increasingly positioned to help enterprises implement integrated security architectures, manage continuous monitoring and translate security findings into actionable risk reduction.

Anh Tien Vu, Industry Principal, Global Cybersecurity, Frost & Sullivan, commented:

"The cloud security market is moving beyond visibility, posture, and fragmented control toward the unified extended cloud security platform model that connects code, cloud, runtime, data, identity, AI, and SOC workflows. The next phase of growth will be defined by platforms that do not simply find risk, but validate and prioritize it, assign ownership, accelerate remediation, and support real-time threat detection and response across complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments."

While North America is expected to remain the largest regional market, expanding cloud adoption, regulatory pressures and demand for managed security capabilities will continue to generate opportunities across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.

As cloud environments become increasingly interconnected and AI-driven, Frost & Sullivan expects competitive differentiation to depend less on the volume of threats identified and more on the ability to translate security intelligence into measurable risk reduction and operational resilience.

#5552. Medical AI startup Boltz raises $110M to speed up small molecule research

Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

Bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of new and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

Boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

Binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

Boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the company, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

Scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

The company also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a new drug.

Usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The company says that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

Boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 launched in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

The company will use its new funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. The extra hardware should make it easier for Boltz to keep up with leading AI labs such as newly public Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group. Over the past year, both companies have introduced models that are highly adapted to biology research tasks.

Boltz has already started training a new generation of molecule design algorithms. The company says that they are “showing substantial improvements” over its current models.
