#5551. Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services

Large national brokerages are expanding into mortgage, title, and servicing to offset thin margins. Several regional firms are opting out, leaning on lender relationships and advertising partnerships while others call ancillaries essential for control and profitability.  AI Summary

It’s no secret that the U.S. housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027. In an attempt to boost ever-tightening margins and claim a larger slice of the transaction pie, many large national brokerages have spent the past year doubling down on ancillary services.

From new mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing, companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform. While this may be the way some of the nation’s largest brokerage companies are thinking about the future, many regional brokerages with strong market share in their states or metros are taking a different tack.

“Our company has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think that we are a residential resale, new development and property management brokerage. Mortgage and title may offer additional income, but our greatest opportunity is to stay relentlessly focused on real estate and be the best at that. I think, when you venture into other arenas, your core gets saturated and your eyes come off the prize.”

Like BHS, Linda O’Koniewski’s RealTrends Verified firm, Leading Edge Real Estate, is also staying out of ancillary services.

“While margins are critically thin for brokerages, and the income would be welcome, we have given it all up,” O’Koniewski said, noting that her company had previously had partnerships with insurance and mortgage companies. “What our clients need is the best loan officer and product. They need a super-responsive insurance agent. We are dedicating ourselves to developing processes and strategies that pre-resolve preventable problems in a transaction and create the best outcomes for our clients.”

O’Koniewski added that her firm’s in-house legal counsel has also suggested homing in on real estate as industries like mortgage and title are not their primary area of expertise.

Although firms like Leading Edge and BHS may not own or have ancillary services joint ventures, this doesn’t mean they lack relationships with lenders or title companies.

At BHS, instead of offering mortgage or title services directly or through a joint venture, the company works with trusted mortgage or title professionals to contribute to the company’s blog, sponsor its podcasts and participate in educational panel discussions.

Leone said BHS works to establish relationships with the top mortgage and title professionals through a “massive in-house commitment to marketing and content creation,” bringing voices from ancillary services industries that BHS feels are the most aligned with its culture and mission.

“They’re providing their expertise to our audience that follows us, as well as providing advertising support to expand the audience that views our 18-plus podcasts and in-house created episodic series shows,” he said. “It is legitimate advertising and earned media exposure at fair market value that allows us to get their expertise to broadcast that to our client base and it also allows us to have an ancillary source of legitimate income.”

Through these posts and marketing material, Leone said BHS is looking to educate its agents and clients, which is why the brokerage likes to partner with creative and experienced ancillary services providers through the program.

“We’re bringing experienced professionals that have seen it all before, and we like to bring those individuals in to get their insights,” Leone said. “Hopefully it allows everyone to stay informed and that is our goal when we’re creating content.”

While not yet as advanced as BHS’s marketing machine, this is what Peter Voss is looking to do with the in-house video production and editing segment he and his team have launched at 3% Listing Co.

“Agents can schedule a time with the in-house video team whenever they want and work with our director on a script and then get in front of the camera and record. We take care of all the editing and produce the video,” Voss said.

Voss said, for his firm, the video production started as a way to provide services to their agents that are beneficial to their business, but also something his firm could afford without significantly increasing overhead costs.

“It is a way to help our agents get their branding out and hopefully generate more transactions, which helps them but also helps our business,” he said.

In the future, Voss said they are looking to expand this service beyond just 3% Listing Co agents, allowing the company to have an additional revenue stream similar to BHS’s operation.

While brokerages like BHS, 3% Listing Co. and Leading Edge may not feel the need to go all-in on ancillary services, Michele Harrington, at First Team Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified firm, sees them as a must-have.

“It is kind of a no-brainer. The profit margins in the real estate brokerage business are just so tiny, so any little bump in the market or a downturn in the market is really going to hurt,” Harrington, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, said.

This is why Harrington believes anyone who owns a brokerage should be exploring ancillary services. Even prior to opening First Team, Harrington, who previously led a 300-agent company based in Southern California, had her own escrow and mortgage companies.

At First Team, Harrington runs an escrow company and a mortgage brokerage operation. She previously had mortgage joint ventures, but said she preferred going the owned mortgage operation route in order to maximize margins.

“The joint venture business isn’t my favorite type of mortgage operation because it is hard to be competitive and have good rates for consumers when everyone involved is trying to make a profit,” she said. “So, your best bet is being a broker where you can go directly to the banks or Rocket or United Wholesale Mortgage and broker the loan. It makes you way more competitive.”

By owning ancillary services, not only can you boost your profit margins, Harrington also feels it enables brokers to provide even better service to consumers.

“It gives you more control. If something goes wrong with escrow or mortgage, the agent calls me, and I tell the president that they need to fix it. That level of control is a nice perk for the agents,” Harrington said.

Beyond providing her agents with more control over transactions, Harrington said having ancillary businesses within her company also helps First Team be more competitive as a brokerage.

“If I want to be more competitive in my splits or be more competitive by offering signing bonuses, I can do those things because ancillary services increase my margins,” she said.

While Voss sees the value of having ancillary services operations, especially when it comes to revenue opportunities, he still doesn’t believe the juice is necessarily worth the squeeze.

“We have talked about bringing mortgage in-house, but what we have found is that in-house operations can be a turn off to a lot of agents,” Voss said. “They feel like it is kind of forced on them to have to send their clients to their firm’s mortgage lender. We are really focused on recruitment right now, so that is why we have shied away from this.”

Leone agrees, telling HousingWire that in-house mortgage or title operations often feel like a “forced option” that agents have to suggest to their clients.

“We don’t want to get in between the relationship of the client and our agent and the agents understand who is best for their client and who is best for that transaction,” he said. “Different lenders make sense for different neighborhoods, price points and scenarios and we don’t want to get in the middle of that.”

Instead Leone and Voss feel that their companies can generate more revenue by focusing on being the best at helping buyers and sellers transact real estate.

“We really focus on our relationships with mortgage lenders and title companies and making sure that we make their jobs easier so that they may be more open to sending business to us and our agents because they know we will get the job done,” Voss said.

#5549. New CEO at Villa eyes manufactured housing, ADU opportunity

Villa hired former Century Communities CFO David Messenger as CEO to scale its ADU and manufactured housing lines. Since 2019, Villa has delivered 425-plus homes and is building projects in Santa Rosa, CA, Altadena, CA and Westminster, CO.  AI Summary

Offsite construction, one of the housing affordability crisis’s hidden-in-plain-sight solutions, gained a blast of momentum this summer when the ROAD Act called for removing the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes. Now, some builders are preparing to capitalize on that growing buzz.

Villa, which operates in California and Colorado, is among them.

Since launching in 2019, the company has delivered more than 425 homes across three core verticals: manufactured single-family communities, ADUs on single-family lots, and ADUs within multifamily communities.

The builder originally focused exclusively on ADUs, but has since expanded into primary homes, delivering its first batch of manufactured single-family houses in Northern California earlier this year. The company is currently building 25 homes in Santa Rosa, California and 14 duplexes in Westminster, Colorado, while also helping rebuild housing for victims of the 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena, California.

The goal now is to scale both the ADU and manufactured housing businesses, with plans for larger single-family communities of up to about 100 lots. To support that growth, Villa announced earlier this week that it hired David Messenger, former CFO of Century Communities, as its next CEO.

For Messenger, moving from one of the country’s largest production homebuilders to an offsite builder focused on ADUs and infill development is quite a pivot. But it also represents an opportunity to focus more on attainable housing in the high-cost areas where Villa operates.

For example, in Santa Rosa, a city of about 180,000 north of San Francisco, the average home price is about $705,000. Comparatively, homes in Villa’s new community, Acacia Village, start at $620,000

“I’ve been drawn to affordable, attainable housing. I think it’s something that the country needs,” Messenger said in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Beyond the opportunity to deliver attainable housing where it’s badly needed, Messenger sees room for growth across all of Villa’s verticals.

“We’ve got three verticals already established. I think all three can continue to grow,” he said.

Villa’s ADU business has plenty of room to grow, Messenger said. Homeowners in California and Colorado are driving strong and growing demand, while California multifamily operators are increasingly building ADUs on open or underutilized land to generate extra rental income.

“More and more multifamily operators see [ADUs] as a way to increase their rental income…at a relatively low cost to their overall project,” Messenger said.

The other growth opportunity is in Villa’s new manufactured home communities. Messenger sees an opening to partner with land developers to build larger communities, potentially with up to around 100 lots. Instead of taking on the expense and risk of acquiring, entitling and developing land themselves, Villa plans to purchase fully entitled and developed land.

“There is an opportunity to work with land developers who, as they’re developing land, are looking for a takeout. The land developers don’t necessarily want to own the land long term. I think if we can provide them a takeout when it’s finished, that is an attractive option for both of us, as we can buy a finished lot. I don’t think that Villa is going to be in the game of developing land, and we’re not looking to take on entitlement risk,” Messenger explained.

Messenger also plans to draw on his experience at Century Communities to help Villa build a more scalable operation. Although the companies operate differently, he believes many of the same production homebuilding principles can apply.

“Having spent 10 years at a production homebuilder, you learn how to establish repeatable processes. Homebuilding involves unpredictable issues every day, so the goal is to make those issues more predictable. Offsite construction lends itself to that because a significant portion of the home is built in a factory, making the process more predictable. It’s about establishing standardized processes that can be repeated for every unit and every lot,” Messenger said.

“Once we get those processes working like a machine, that’s what makes the business scalable,” he added.

As Villa scales, Messenger doesn’t expect production capacity to be an issue. Instead of owning and operating its own factories, the company contracts with reputable, third-party production facilities to build its homes and ADUs.

“We’ve partnered with different factories all over the state of California. We partner with factories in Colorado, Nebraska and Albuquerque for dealing with those projects. We are developing an extensive array of relationships to make sure that we don’t get hamstrung by a capacity problem,” he said.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July, included a provision that removed the decades-long requirement that manufactured homes be built with a permanent steel chassis. The change has received a lot of attention, leading The New York Times to name chassis as its word of the day on November 11.

Manufacturers cite two main benefits of this rule change, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is now finalizing. First, removing the steel chassis gives manufactured homebuilders greater design flexibility, allowing them to build larger, multi-story and more aesthetically appealing homes that more closely resemble traditional site-built housing.

“If you actually walk through a manufactured home product today and look at the finishes being delivered, it’s a completely different product from what people actually think about. If we can do some marketing and outreach and get people in the door to see what these homes look like, I think they’ll be amazed at what they see,” Messenger said.

That added design flexibility could help the industry shed longstanding stigmas and gain acceptance in communities where zoning restrictions historically thwarted manufactured housing, which is typically a more affordable alternative to traditional stick-built homes.

Manufacturers also see an opportunity to expand into high-cost urban and suburban infill markets, where multi-story designs can make higher-density development more economically feasible. Villa, which operates in high-cost cities with limited developable land, is among the homebuilders positioned to benefit from this rule change.

“As we’re evaluating communities, not having a chassis requirement should open up more lots and communities where we can build on,” Messenger said. “I think it provides additional opportunities for us.”

#5548. Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid

Financial software company Intuit Inc. today announced that it has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian technology holding company Bending Spoons S.p.A. for about $3.68 billion.

Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the company paid. The 2021 purchase was the largest in Intuit’s history at the time.

Although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares. That leaves Intuit with $3.31 billion in cash from the sale, according to the companies. Included in the deal is The Rocket Science Group LLC, the legal entity behind Mailchimp. Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

Selling Mailchimp is said to sharpen Intuit’s focus on the artificial intelligence-native tools it has built to help businesses win new customers, manage their pipeline and grow. Once the deal closes, Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to buy back its own shares before the end of fiscal 2027.

Jack Tam, a senior vice president at Intuit, said the company is confident Bending Spoons “will lead Mailchimp to continued success in this next chapter.”

Growth at Mailchimp has stalled in recent quarters. Revenue from the business fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended Oct. 31. Intuit’s full-year guidance has Mailchimp revenue coming in flat to down 1%. In November 2024, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla told analysts that Intuit was seeing higher churn from smaller Mailchimp customers.

“Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences,” said Luca Ferrari, co-founder and chief executive of Bending Spoons. “We’re honored to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together.”

Ferrari added that Bending Spoons plans to invest substantially in Mailchimp after closing. According to Bending Spoons, the transformation of a business it acquires is typically deep, entailing reorganized teams, overhauled technology and redesigned user interfaces.

Founded in 2013, Bending Spoons has built a portfolio of digital businesses that includes AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo and WeTransfer. Since listing on the Nasdaq in July, the company has also completed acquisitions of Airtable Inc. for $1.285 billion and whiteboard platform Miro for $1.355 billion.

Intuit announced the sale alongside its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results. For the quarter, it reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91, up 56% from $1.87 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $4.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting adjusted earnings of $2.70 per share on revenue of $4.31 billion.

For its fiscal second quarter, Intuit expects adjusted earnings per share of $3.17 to $3.22 on revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion. Intuit lowered its full-year revenue guidance to between $23.08 billion and $23.37 billion.

Behind the cut is Credit Karma, the company’s personal finance and credit score service, which is now forecast to grow 3% to 7% this fiscal year, down from 11% to 13% previously. Intuit reiterated its full-year adjusted earnings guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 per share. None of the guidance includes the effect of the Mailchimp sale.

Intuit shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading.

#5547. Trump's H-1B crackdown is pushing skilled tech workers to leave the U.S.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

IBM is ending visa sponsorship for most consulting jobs while the Labor Department proposes tighter permanent residency rules

Yash Sharma, a Google $GOOGL software engineer from India, plans to leave the U.S. for the U.K. next month after six years on an H-1B visa, according to Bloomberg. Sharma, 36, cited repeated changes to visa rules and slim odds of becoming a citizen.

The U.K. approved Sharma for a Global Talent visa that lets him move without a job offer, according to Bloomberg. His application for a U.S. "extraordinary ability" visa was turned down following a lengthy wait, and he has avoided traveling abroad for the past 18 months out of concern that he would not be allowed back in. He told Bloomberg the U.S. feels like a "golden prison."

The Labor Department proposed a rule earlier this week for the permanent labor certification program. It would strengthen recruitment standards and recordkeeping requirements and eliminate administrative exemptions to the labor market test, the agency said. The department called it the first comprehensive set of reforms to the program in nearly 20 years, and comments are open through Jan. 19, 2027.

Employers are adjusting as well. IBM $IBM said it is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting, its largest division. Affected workers can either continue with IBM from a location abroad or depart the firm before the year ends.

Boston-based Flywire disclosed in its quarterly report this month that it is considering shifting its hiring and product development to cheaper locations as a way to absorb rising H-1B visa expenses, according to Bloomberg.

The Trump administration started by issuing a proclamation that demanded $100,000 for some would-be employees living abroad, according to Bloomberg. Even though a court had halted that payment, it announced a different $103,000 charge on new H-1B applications in August.

The Labor Department last month barred Microsoft $MSFT, Adobe $ADBE and a set of large IT outsourcing companies from the Permanent Labor Certification program because of ongoing federal investigations, according to Bloomberg. Deputy Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspensions.

The U.S. handed out roughly 260,000 fewer short-term, non-immigrant visas in the 2025 budget year compared with the previous one, according to Bloomberg, citing Migration Policy Institute analysis of federal data. That year still counted the final three complete months of former President Joe Biden’s time in office. New foreign student enrollment at U.S. universities is down an estimated 15% this fall, according to Bloomberg, citing the Institute of International Education.

According to Bloomberg, the administration contends that for years both employers and workers have exploited the immigration system, which it says has depressed wages for Americans.

Chris Thomas, an immigration lawyer and partner at Holland & Hart, told Bloomberg that some corporate clients are saying "it's too much, it's time to start offshoring." Kate Angustia, supervisory policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, told Bloomberg: “We are creating a brain drain.”

#5546. AlphaPoint Introduces Approval Device to Help Protect Businesses in an Era of AI-Driven Threats

Dedicated hardware lets authorized employees review and approve sensitive requests separately from their computers, adding an independent checkpoint as attacks become harder to spot.

NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AlphaPoint, a provider of institutional digital asset infrastructure since 2013, today introduced the Approval Device, a dedicated hardware device with its own secure display and an optional FIPS 140-3-certified secure element, designed to help businesses protect their most sensitive actions in an increasingly hostile, AI-driven threat environment.

Designed to integrate with existing systems, the Approval Device adds a hacker-resistant approval step to the workflows that matter most, such as administrative changes, payments and access to sensitive data. AI hacking makes laptops, workstations and mobile phones vulnerable, and the Approval Device helps protect administrative and security-critical workflows. Its software is written using security-first best practices and formally verified programming languages for safety and correctness, and it uses no complex operating system such as Linux, Windows or macOS, keeping its attack surface to an absolute minimum.

Even if an attacker has taken over an employee's other work devices, the Approval Device clearly shows the action about to be processed. Hardware wallets protect cryptocurrency transactions the same way, and the Approval Device brings that model to traditional business workflows beyond the blockchain.

An easy-to-use SDK lets human and AI programmers connect the device to the processes that matter most to your business. Once connected, it protects them from employee system compromise.

AlphaPoint is providing an evaluation kit to businesses, please contact us for more information.

Employee systems can perform consequential actions through business administration software, websites, and mobile applications. Multi-party approval flows offer enhanced security and continuity. During onboarding, humans and AI systems help identify what needs protection and who can approve those actions.

When one of those actions is requested, the designated approvers review it on the device's own screen and deliberately hold to approve or decline. A compromised computer can show one request while submitting another, but the device shows only the real one, and each approval is cryptographically bound to that exact request. Policy controls then confirm every required approval is in place before the action goes ahead.

"Attackers keep winning with the same classes of vulnerabilities. They rarely need anything new, because the old weaknesses keep working. We decided to stop fighting them one patch at a time. The Approval Device is designed to take entire classes of attack off the table, not just the latest example of each. That means a far smaller attack surface, far fewer ways in, and employee systems that are far harder to compromise," said Joe Ventura, CTO of AlphaPoint.

Potential applications include changes to administrative permissions, updates to critical system settings, releases of sensitive information and transfers of funds. Organizations can define approval requirements around the consequences of an action, including additional approvers for higher-risk requests.

The Approval Device works with Secure Core, which is designed to keep sensitive business logic, data and credentials separate from everyday application systems, protect keys in hardware, and keep signed, exportable records of every approval.

AlphaPoint works as a design partner to identify the workflows an organization needs to protect, define approval policies and support integration and validation within its existing systems. A 30-minute security briefing under NDA provides an opportunity to review the architecture, threat model and verification evidence.

To arrange a call, visit alphapoint.com/alphapoint-cloud. Qualified companies receive a free evaluation kit containing physical equipment for evaluation.

#5545. Rate’s Jesse Allen: Reverse mortgage lenders should plan for the ‘down case,’ not FHA relief

Jesse Allen of Rate said lenders should expand reverse mortgage product menus to reduce reliance on FHA-backed HECMs. He said proprietary reverse is about 40% of Rate originations and that Rate is also growing its HECM volume year over year.  AI Summary

With mortgage lenders continuing to cut expenses, including personnel, as the originations forecast for 2027 dims, Jesse Allen said the reverse mortgage business at Rate is still growing and he isn’t waiting for federal housing leaders to offer help.

At last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association Annual Meeting & Expo, Allen said he’s planning for the “down case” on Federal Housing Administration policy regarding upfront mortgage insurance premiums (MIP) for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). Allen’s comments came not long after Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley said the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with current MIP structures for FHA-insured single-family home loans and reverse mortgages.

“In an uncertain environment, you have to plan and execute to your down case scenarios, and then when something better than down case happens, you’re that much better,” Allen said.

Allen, the president of the 55+ lending division at Rate and a NRMLA board member for 2026-27, sat down with HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily at NRMLA Annual to discuss some of the hot topics of interest for industry professionals. He said that lenders should look to expand their product menus to insulate themselves from any obstacles to federally insured loans, and he pitched responsible home equity release as the next big opportunity for the wider mortgage industry.

NRMLA and other trade groups have spent the past year arguing that the FHA could lower the upfront mortgage insurance premium for certain borrowers. Allen said that cutting some fees would pull more people into the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, which he called “basic insurance economics.” NRMLA has also laid out the math to lower premiums for borrowers who utilize less of their HECM proceeds while lobbying to eliminate second appraisals.

But with the political transition underway after the recent midterm elections, Allen does not expect quick action. “I’m not building my business model or business case around that,” he said. “If positive things happen, it’s wind in the sails.”

Still, a lower upfront MIP could be “powerful for older homeowners” who want to access their equity responsibly, he said, as they might tap 30% to 40% of their available line of credit now while saving the rest for later in retirement.

When asked whether he thinks a more balanced Congress is coming in 2027, Allen said everyone’s definition of balanced differs. But he also believes that if Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) takes over the Senate banking committee, “we’re going to see more regulatory interest.” Allen’s approach, he added, is to operate daily as though auditors are showing up, which should be the standard for a business that serves a protected class of senior homeowners.

Allen clarified that Rate is a nondelegated correspondent lender for proprietary reverse mortgage products and is fully delegated on FHA-backed HECM products. Proprietary loans make up about 40% of Rate’s reverse mortgage originations, he said, and he estimated them at 55% to 65% of its volume based on their typically larger loan sizes.

Similar to the industry at large, private-label loans are where growth is happening at Rate, although its HECM volume is rising too, Allen said, with the company outpacing the industry year over year. According to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight, Rate was the 13th-largest HECM lender in the country through the first nine months of the year, with its 228 endorsements up 41% compared to the same period in 2025.

Proprietary loans often serve borrowers that FHA products can’t, including owners of high-value homes and those who want to pay off consumer debt without it counting against them in qualification — a guideline NRMLA has pushed to change. But Allen said his team spends time reminding loan officers that the HECM is “still an awesome product.”

Compared with a traditional home equity line of credit, he said, a HECM line of credit mitigates the risk that falling home values lead to frozen lines, leaving borrowers without access when “they need their equity the most.” HECM lines of credit can grow for the life of the loan if the borrower doesn’t exhaust funds and meets requirements like property tax and insurance payments. Proprietary lines of credit typically stop growing after seven to 10 years, Allen added.

Allen pointed to reverse for purchase financing as a tool for addressing affordability. He said that one of Rate’s top loan officers recently closed a reverse for purchase for the parent of one of his real estate agent partners. The LO had a couple of reverse mortgages under his belt but had never done a purchase deal, and he worked with one of the company’s specialists to get it done.

“Specialty lending in general is a big priority for most mortgage companies today,” Allen said, naming non-QM and builder programs alongside reverse.

Allen thinks that today’s retirees are less willing to sacrifice their lifestyles. Reverse mortgage proceeds can fund a variety of uses — from family vacations to in-home care that eases the load on adult children, or even a move into a 55-plus community without draining savings.

“That’s why I love this business, because it’s infinitely customizable,” he said. “Every client is unique, every situation is unique, and we have this expanding suite of products to really help deliver for the clients … so that they can get the joy out of the transaction.”

#5544. Lufthansa is cutting 1,000 jobs at its flagship airline amid fuel cost pain

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Lufthansa Airlines plans the cuts at its Munich and Frankfurt hubs along with less short- and medium-haul capacity and a smaller A320 fleet

Lufthansa Group will eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its flagship Lufthansa Airlines unit, where expensive fuel is adding pressure to the loss-making mainline carrier, according to Bloomberg and France 24.

The positions are at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to Bloomberg. The cuts equal about 2.5% of the airline's roughly 40,000 employees, according to France 24.

Lufthansa Airlines intends to fly fewer short- and medium-haul services, downsize its Airbus A320 fleet and shift toward the smaller A220, according to Bloomberg. A management letter to employees outlining the plan was signed by the airline's top executives, including CEO Jens Ritter, Bloomberg said.

"After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future," management wrote in the letter, according to Bloomberg. The letter cited the war in the Middle East, high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and the airline's cost base as factors that worsened the situation in 2026.

Over the first nine months, Lufthansa Airlines lost €180 million ($202 million) at the operating level, according to Bloomberg. Management does not expect significant earnings contributions from the airline in the fourth quarter, Bloomberg said.

The cuts land while Lufthansa is working to end a standoff with its pilots. The company submitted an offer to the Vereinigung Cockpit pilots' union on Tuesday that includes as many as 1,000 new pilot hires by the end of 2033, pay raises beginning in 2029 and one-off payments.

The union said it has not reached an agreement and set Nov. 23 as the deadline for Lufthansa to reconsider. Pilot strikes have cost Lufthansa more than €200 million ($224 million), according to Bloomberg.

The wider group saw profit climb 30% in the July-September period, helped by passengers who kept buying premium seats on long-haul flights. Its annual fuel bill is projected to run €2 billion ($2.24 billion) above the 2025 level, France 24 said. Lufthansa has twice cut its full-year profit outlook and anticipates heavier fuel costs again in 2027, according to Bloomberg.

The group announced plans in September 2025 to eliminate 4,000 administrative positions by 2030, according to Bloomberg. It was unclear whether the job reductions announced Friday fall under that plan or come on top of it, according to France 24. A Lufthansa spokesman would not elaborate, France 24 said.

Lufthansa stock slid by up to 1.7% during the opening hours of Frankfurt trading on Friday. It was up 5.3% for the year as of Thursday's close.

#5543. Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate

Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine update to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk.

Researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space.

How the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday.

The researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

The malware itself is delivered through a .pth file added to both releases, a type of file Python runs every time it starts, meaning the credential stealer runs even if the framework itself is never imported. The two versions also kept the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0 as a dependency, so the framework continued to work normally while the malware ran in the background.

Once running, the malware collects secrets from environment variables and from other running processes, along with credential files for services such as Azure, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face. It also requests Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, according to application security company Endor Labs Inc., with the second version adding requests for GitHub Actions tokens. The stolen data is then compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site address controlled by the attacker.

Researchers at malware tracking site OpenSourceMalware described the malware as a “focused credential and token stealer, not a remote access trojan,” noting that it does not install any persistence on infected systems.

Wiz’s analysis suggests the number of victims may be small, though it covers only the 50 requests the attacker’s free webhook.site account retained. Of those, 17 represented only three unique successful thefts of victim data, with the rest coming from the attacker’s own machines and from sandbox and security vendor scanning.

The incident is not the first this year involving an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Microsoft’s durabletask package was hijacked after its PyPI token was stolen in an attack that has been linked to TeamPCP, the group also behind the compromise of LiteLLM. Wiz says it has not linked the two incidents.

Anyone who installed either of the malicious versions is being urged to treat it as a credential compromise, according to researchers, who recommend rebuilding from version 1.26.0 and rotating any secrets the affected systems could access.

“A list of dependencies in production might show no trace of the framework, while a build runner could have installed it and been shut down before the alert arrived,” James Matchett, head of security at software supply chain security company Cloudsmith Ltd., told SiliconANGLE.

“If that runner had access to a deployment token, the team needs to know which version it installed and what the token could access,” he added.

#5542. In HelloNation, Digital Marketing Expert Sean O'Kelly Outlines Realistic Timelines for Local Business SEO in West Virginia

Most Local Businesses in West Virginia Can Expect Measurable SEO Improvements Within Three to Six Months of Consistent Effort.

CHARLESTON, W. Va., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How long does it realistically take for a local business in West Virginia to see results from search engine optimization? A HelloNation article addresses this question with a practical look at SEO timelines, explaining the variables that shape how quickly local business SEO efforts begin to show measurable returns.

The article explains that for most businesses in the state, measurable improvements tend to appear within three to six months of consistent work. That range is intentionally wide. It reflects the number of variables involved, including where the website starts, how competitive the market is, and the quality of the optimization effort itself.

Where a business begins matters significantly. A company that has never invested in SEO starts with little to no domain authority, minimal indexed content, and no established backlink profile. A business with an existing website has a foundation to build from, even if it has been neglected for some time. The gap between those two situations directly affects how quickly early progress becomes visible.

Competition shapes the timeline as well. In smaller West Virginia markets, a business offering a niche service in a specific county may see local business SEO results more quickly than a business chasing broad terms in a larger metro area. The article notes that targeting well-defined, locally specific keywords consistently outperforms trying to rank for national or highly competitive terms in the early stages of a campaign.

Website quality is another factor. Search engines evaluate how fast a site loads, how well it functions on mobile devices, and how easy it is to crawl and index. A site with significant technical issues may see slower progress even when other optimization work is being done well.

Digital Marketing Expert Sean O'Kelly's insights, as featured in the article, make clear that the early months of a local business SEO campaign in West Virginia require patience. Initial results are often incremental. A business might begin appearing in results for terms where it previously had no presence at all, or see rankings move from a deeper page toward the first. This early progress is meaningful, even if it does not immediately translate into more calls or form submissions.

Traffic growth generally follows ranking improvements by several weeks. As rankings stabilize in stronger positions, more users see and click the result. As more users visit and engage with the site, those behavioral signals reinforce the ranking further. The process compounds over time, which is one reason consistency matters so much throughout the early stages.

Businesses that pause local business SEO efforts during the first few months often find they are restarting the clock when they resume. Search engines respond to sustained signals of relevance and credibility. Inconsistent effort tends to produce inconsistent results. By the six-to-twelve-month mark, a business that has stayed committed to on-page optimization, local citation building, content creation, and technical maintenance typically sees meaningful traffic growth and a measurable increase in leads from organic search. For most markets in West Virginia, the competitive landscape is manageable enough that a well-executed strategy can build a clear advantage within a year.

Local Business SEO in West Virginia: A Realistic Look at Results and Timelines features insights from Sean O'Kelly, Digital Marketing Expert of Charleston, West Virginia, in HelloNation.

#5541. Texas’ population boom is opening doors for new real estate agents

Texas added 391,243 people in 12 months and authorized 210,217 new-home permits in 2025

Few states are changing as quickly as Texas. It added more people than any other state between 2024 and 2025, and builders there got the green light for more new homes in 2025 than anywhere else in the country. More people and more houses mean more deals to be done, and more room for new agents to get in on them.

Texas’ population has passed 31 million, and the suburbs surrounding Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio are stretching farther and farther out. Competition has cooled compared with the pandemic boom, yet the demand behind the market continues to climb.

Expensive markets with little buildable land work differently. In Texas, the business depends on sheer size, people relocating and a pipeline of newly built homes.

Over the 12 months ending July 2025, Texas grew by 391,243 people, a bigger gain than any other state posted. The population now sits near 31.7 million, 8.8% higher than in 2020.

Each newcomer is a future tenant, homebuyer or seller, and many will start households of their own. That means agents don’t have to count on climbing prices for opportunity. The bigger driver is people relocating and settling in for the long haul.

Raw population counts miss how often Texans relocate. In 2024, the state accounted for 7.8% of every move between states, a share topped only by Florida. Meanwhile, 3.4 million residents changed addresses without leaving Texas, the highest in-state figure in the nation.

More newcomers still come from California than from anywhere else. Once all the arrivals and departures between states are netted out, Texas came out roughly 73,000 residents ahead.

All that activity is what keeps agents busy. A client arriving from out of state and one moving a few miles away both need help, which gives relocation-focused agents a reliable stream of business in and around the big metros.

Look at every U.S. city with 20,000 or more residents, and the five growing fastest are all in Texas. Fulshear, outside Houston, is the only one that isn’t in the Dallas-Fort Worth orbit.

Austin hit 1 million residents that same year, becoming the fifth Texas city of that size alongside Houston, San Antonio, Dallas and Fort Worth. For new real estate agents, though, the bigger openings are in suburbs, master-planned developments and up-and-coming markets, not city centers.

No state approved permits for more new homes in 2025 than Texas, which authorized 210,217 units. Dallas and Houston ranked first and second among all U.S. metros, with Austin seventh.

All three metros issued fewer permits than in 2024, yet each is still well ahead of most of the nation. Whole subdivisions are under construction right now, and that work supports agents who sell new builds, partner with builders, focus on master-planned communities, help relocating families or guide people buying their first home.

Statewide active listings were up 2.8% in Q3 2026, and 18 of Texas’ 26 metros saw inventory increase. The median price across the state dipped 0.4% to $333,628, even as 15 metros posted price gains and 12 recorded more sales.

That extra selection lets buyers shop around. Sellers, meanwhile, are counting on their agents to set a smart price, present the home well, get it seen and negotiate effectively.

Among Texas REALTORS® surveyed in 2026, 69% said their buyers faced no competing offers, compared with 57% a year earlier. Seventy-one percent described buyers’ search timelines as ample or reasonable, and only 6% blamed a stalled search on thin inventory.

That changes what clients need from an agent. Outbidding the competition matters less than helping buyers choose well. The agents who stand out have deep neighborhood knowledge, can lay out what different homes will really cost each month and know how to get the most out of builder incentives.

Being a trusted advisor counts for more than processing forms.

International purchasers bought roughly 7,780 Texas homes from April 2025 through March 2026, spending a combined $4 billion. Texas captured 12% of the nation’s international homebuyers over that stretch.

Buyers from Mexico made up the biggest group, with India, China, Nigeria and the U.K. rounding out the top five. More than half, 58%, settled in the suburbs. Agents comfortable with overseas relocations and cross-border transactions have an expanding specialty to tap into, and much of it is in suburban markets.

Texas leaves plenty of room to shape your own business. One agent might become the go-to expert in a single booming suburb. Another might focus on new construction where builders are most active, or on families arriving from out of state or relocating within Texas.

Other specialties are open too, from international clients to first-time buyers, move-up buyers and rental investors. You also get to decide whether you’d rather work in a large metro or one of the state’s smaller fast-growing towns.

Whichever direction you choose, expect paychecks to be inconsistent at first. Every specialty depends on regular lead generation and on building relationships over time.

Texas requires aspiring agents to finish 180 hours of qualifying education before they can be licensed. Colibri Real Estate delivers those courses online, so you can fit your studies around the job you already have.

If you choose a package with exam prep, you’ll also get practice exams and live sessions where instructors answer your questions, all aimed at getting you ready to pass.

Building a real estate career in Texas takes effort, and your first years will be spent generating leads and growing your business. Still, if you’re ready to do that work, the conditions are strong: millions of residents relocating, suburbs springing up and homebuilding happening on a massive scale.

New households and new housing markets keep appearing across Texas. For agents committed to the work, there’s plenty of room to grow alongside them.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Anthropic stock fell 8% in premarket trading on Friday after closing up 17% at $97.17 a share in its first day on the Nasdaq

Anthropic stock fell 8% in premarket trading on Friday, a day after the AI lab debuted on the Nasdaq $NDAQ in the largest initial public offering on record.

The stock was down 8.1% at 7:05 a.m. ET. Nvidia $NVDA stock fell 2.4% and AMD $AMD stock fell 6.8% as fears about AI continued to fuel a selloff, according to CNBC.

AMD stock ended Thursday more than 7% lower after Hunterbrook Media published a report claiming that AMD firmware had been found at companies on U.S. blacklists, and its affiliate Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position, according to CNBC. AMD told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Anthropic opened trading on the Nasdaq at $111.50 on Thursday under the ticker ANT, 34% above its $83 IPO price. The offering topped the $75 billion SpaceX raised at the start of its June IPO. Anthropic stock hit a high of $115.10 after the open and at one point fell below $100.

#5539. Resolve AI’s SRE-1 model finds root causes of production alerts as AI agents go on call

Incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

The new model, announced Wednesday, reflects the company’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan said Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

In testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

Primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in production are said to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

Salesforce Inc. is among the early users. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, said that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”

“No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” said Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”

Primary On-call is now generally available. Access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI’s own platform.

Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

#5538. Ezee Fiber Wins Two 2026 Fierce Network Innovation Awards

New Mexico fiber expansion named Broadband Build of the Year;

CEO Matt Marino named Innovator of the Year

HOUSTON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ezee Fiber won two categories in the 2026 Fierce Network Innovation Awards, a leading telecommunications industry awards program. Its fiber-to-the-home expansion in Albuquerque and Santa Fe was named Broadband Build of the Year, and CEO Matt Marino was named Innovator of the Year.

The awards were announced and presented Nov. 19 during Broadband Nation Expo at the Hilton Riverside in New Orleans. The ceremony marked the first live, in-person presentation of the awards in the program's more than 15-year history.

New Mexico build recognized for measurable community impact

The Broadband Build of the Year category honors completed builds with measurable community results. At the end of 2022, only about 4% of Bernalillo County and 9% of Santa Fe County could buy fiber at home. Ezee Fiber's $250 million New Mexico expansion, announced in 2023, now offers symmetrical residential speeds up to 8 Gbps and enterprise connectivity up to 400 Gbps, with no data caps.

A July 2026 Ezee Fiber-sponsored study by Dr. Brian Whitacre of Oklahoma State University ties roughly 661 local jobs to the rollout from 2021 to 2024 and estimates $77 million in home-value gains through 2025. More than 95% of the company's New Mexico roles are filled locally, and it has invested $98 million in in-state supply chain spending.

After a 2025 stop-work order in Albuquerque, Ezee Fiber worked with city leaders on "neighbor-first" construction protocols that cut construction-related 311 calls by 47% year over year.

"This award belongs to our New Mexico team," said Pedro Checo, chief operating officer of Ezee Fiber. "New Mexico shows what fiber can do when it's built with local people, local partners and a long-term commitment to the community."

Since joining as CEO in 2023, Marino has built Ezee Fiber around the customer experience, pairing fast, reliable fiber with 24/7 local customer service. Under his leadership, that model is expanding from Texas and New Mexico into Washington, Illinois, Oregon and Michigan.

"Together, these awards recognize the commitment of our teams to building better networks, delivering exceptional service and earning the trust of customers and communities," Marino said. "Innovation is not simply about technology. It is about how effectively we deliver on our promises, solve problems and create lasting value for the people we serve."

The recognition marks the inaugural presentation of Fierce Network's Innovator of the Year award and highlights the growing influence of emerging fiber providers in an industry historically dominated by much larger companies.

Hiring and recognition continue as the industry contracts

Fierce Network honors add to a growing list of national industry recognitions for Ezee Fiber. PCMag named the company the best overall internet service provider in the U.S. for 2026 and included it among the Best Gaming ISPs (2025, 2026) and Fastest ISPs in the U.S. (2024, 2025).

Ezee Fiber has also earned 65 Speedtest by Ookla awards. A recent edition of Consumer Reports ranked Ezee Fiber among the nation's top 10 internet providers, with consumers praising its value, pricing and simplicity.

The recognition comes as Ezee Fiber continues to expand its network, customer base and workforce across six states. While several major U.S. telecommunications companies have announced substantial workforce reductions, Ezee Fiber continues to invest in new markets and hire employees in sales, field operations, customer service and other functions. The company employs approximately 800 people and is targeting 200,000 customers and 800,000 homes passed by the end of 2026.

For more information about Ezee Fiber and service availability, visit www.ezeefiber.com.

Ezee Fiber is a rapidly growing fiber internet company delivering premium multi-gigabit service to residential, business and government customers over a 100% fiber-optic network at exceptional value. The company's carrier-grade infrastructure spans Texas, New Mexico, Illinois, Oregon, Michigan and Washington, supported by local teams who live and work in the communities they serve. Ezee Fiber's industry-leading speeds, award-winning customer service and transparent pricing model set the company apart. Learn more at www.ezeefiber.com.

#5537. Ex-Alibaba AI chief's startup Pragmatik Labs closed funding at $5B value

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Shanghai-based AI agent developer was valued at $2 billion in August, when it raised several hundred million dollars

Pragmatik Labs, launched by Lin Junyang after he served as Alibaba Group Holding's top AI executive, has secured a funding round that values it at $5 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The valuation is up from $2 billion in August, when the company completed its first financing, according to Bloomberg. That first round raised several hundred million dollars. The new round brought in tens of millions of dollars.

New investors include HyT Capital, CDH Investments and automaker Geely Automobile Holdings, according to Bloomberg. Representatives for Pragmatik, HyT, CDH and Geely did not respond to requests for comment from Bloomberg.

Pragmatik, a Shanghai company nicknamed p7k, develops AI agents that operate in virtual settings as well as real-world ones. Investors that took part in the first round were Gaorong Ventures, HSG, Tencent Holdings and Shanghai Engine Fund, an investment arm supported by the city government, according to Bloomberg.

Lin set up Pragmatik over the summer after leaving Alibaba, according to Bloomberg. He gets credit for overseeing the creation of Alibaba's Qwen family of large language models, which went on to underpin the company's main AI apps and services.

Lin is one of several Chinese artificial intelligence researchers who have launched research-oriented companies, called neolabs, aiming to take on established players such as DeepSeek and Moonshot, according to Bloomberg. The group is following a path laid by American researchers including Ilya Sutskever and Yann LeCun, both of whom quit large technology companies to found ventures of their own.

The neolabs want to emulate what Anthropic and OpenAI have achieved, but within narrower specialties such as equipping AI with an understanding of the physical world or creating coding systems that can improve on their own, according to Bloomberg.

Lin has said China probably will not overtake Anthropic and OpenAI within the coming three to five years, since computing resources are limited, according to Bloomberg.

#5536. Vitalik Buterin Wants Crypto to Have Housing’s Stability, But Can Ethereum Deliver?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin believes younger generations investing in stocks and digital assets instead of housing could help ease pressure on property prices. However, he says crypto still needs something that makes housing attractive: stability.

Buterin thinks that housing creates incentives for owners to keep property prices high, even when cheaper homes would benefit society. Digital assets could offer an alternative, but today’s platforms often encourage excessive speculation.

“We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets,” Buterin wrote on X

His comments raise a question for Ethereum. Can the network evolve beyond speculative trading and become dependable infrastructure for people building long-term digital wealth?

One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities.That…

Ethereum’s development roadmap increasingly focuses on making the network faster, more efficient, and harder to disrupt. Its next major upgrade, Glamsterdam, is in testing, and ethereum.org lists a mainnet launch for Q4 2026 with no date confirmed yet. The upgrade introduces several changes designed to improve Ethereum’s capacity without sacrificing decentralization.

One major feature is Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS). It moves the relationship between block proposers and builders directly into Ethereum’s protocol, reducing reliance on external relays and additional trust assumptions.

Another important development is Block-Level Access Lists. The feature prepares Ethereum to process unrelated transactions in parallel rather than handling everything sequentially.

These improvements could help Ethereum support more financial applications while keeping its infrastructure accessible to independent node operators. So, if digital assets are expected to become long-term financial instruments rather than vehicles for short-term speculation, this is very much needed.

Ethereum also provides an established foundation for staking, stablecoins, decentralized lending, and tokenized real-world assets. These applications could give investors more ways to hold and use digital wealth without constantly trading volatile tokens.

Yet, security, reliable applications, and responsible financial products must develop alongside network capacity.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Ethereum’s market performance presents a contrasting picture. ETH is trading just a notch above $1,800. This leaves the coin 63% below its all-time high of $4,946. The decline highlights the gap between Ethereum’s technological ambitions and its current market valuation.

Ethereum’s network utility and ETH’s investment performance are also not interchangeable. More applications and transactions can strengthen the ecosystem, but they do not create proportional demand for ETH.

The token still plays an important role as Ethereum’s native transaction currency, staking asset, and collateral across decentralized finance. For this reason, continued growth in staking, stablecoins, and tokenized assets could strengthen ETH’s underlying investment narrative.

Buterin’s comments are bigger than a debate about housing affordability. He is effectively challenging the crypto industry to build assets and platforms that encourage long-term ownership rather than constant speculation.

Ethereum has several pieces of that foundation already, including proof-of-stake security, smart contracts, and an expanding financial ecosystem.

Its upcoming upgrades aim to improve the infrastructure supporting those applications. But the network still needs to prove that its technology can deliver dependable financial products at scale.

#5535. Which way is down, revisited

Mortgage delinquencies are rising year over year, but nominal home prices are still up nationally. Compared with 2008, distress is more concentrated by loan type and market, suggesting delinquency-to-price signals may depend on local regime conditions.   AI Summary

In 2008, HousingWire published an analysis asking whether severe mortgage delinquencies were pushing home prices down, or falling prices were pushing delinquencies up.

Seventeen of 20 major metros showed a significant negative correlation between 60-plus-day delinquencies and Case-Shiller prices. Granger causality tests found delinquency trends and predicted price trends in 13 metros; six showed a two-way relationship, and only San Francisco showed prices leading delinquencies. In most markets, distress appeared to be part of the mechanism driving prices lower.

The 2026 market looks very different. Delinquencies are rising year over year while nominal prices still rise nationally. The 2008 relationship may not have vanished, but the housing-credit system may have moved into a different causal regime.

The Mortgage Bankers Association reported a 4.37% national delinquency rate in the second quarter, 44 basis points above a year earlier. The 90-day rate edged up to 1.43%, foreclosures stood at 0.67% of loans and the seriously delinquent rate rose for a fourth straight quarter.

Yet the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller National Index rose 1.9% year over year in July, the 20-City Composite 2.5% and FHFA’s index 2.6%. Prices have fallen in real terms for 14 straight months, though much of July’s 3.4% inflation was energy-driven; core inflation was 2.5%. The market combines nominal stability, real erosion and rising credit stress, a configuration unlike 2008.

Conventional delinquency was 2.72%, VA 4.89% and FHA 11.79%, with FHA up 122 basis points in a year. ATTOM counted 40,277 foreclosure filings in August, up 13%, with completed foreclosures up 42%. Activity remains far below the 2008–2010 crisis, which helps explain why rising delinquency has not collapsed prices.

Equity is also uneven. ATTOM found 3.2% of mortgaged homes seriously underwater in the second quarter, up from 2.7% a year earlier. Minnesota led at 12.1%, up from 2.6%, while second-ranked Louisiana, at 10.3%, improved from 11.9%. Underwater share measures vulnerability, not distress itself.

Chicago led the Case-Shiller metros in July at 6.9%; Seattle (−1.6), Las Vegas (−1.3) and Denver (−1.1) declined. That 8.5-point spread reflects different regimes within one national economy. A market can carry distress without falling prices if supply is tight, and a falling market can breed delinquency if equity is thin. The relevant unit is the local borrower-market system, not the nation.

The 2008 mechanism was distressed supply: delinquency, foreclosures and REO, lower prices, lower equity, more delinquency. It remains valid, but today’s distressed pipeline is far smaller, so the default-to-price channel may be weaker in aggregate. The reverse channel, in which lower prices erode equity and raise default incentives for leveraged borrowers, may matter more.

The better question is no longer which comes first, but under what conditions the direction changes. One hypothesis: in a normal regime the link is weak; in an equity-stress regime falling prices drive delinquency; in a distressed-supply regime concentrated delinquency drives prices; in a feedback regime both operate at once. That is a framework to test, not a finding.

Whether the 2008 relationship holds today is untested; I am not aware of a published re-estimation across the post-crisis period.

A modern version should use metro-level price and delinquency series from roughly 2000 to 2026, retain the Granger framework for comparability, test for cointegration, add controls for unemployment, mortgage rates, loan type, leverage and equity, and test whether coefficients shift once thresholds such as cumulative price declines, negative equity or serious delinquency are crossed.

This article does not replicate the original tests, which used proprietary loan-level data; comparable public metro delinquency series are not available in the same form.

In 2008, delinquency, foreclosure and falling prices reinforced one another nationally. In 2026, credit stress is rising while nominal prices hold and metros diverge. The evidence suggests the relationship may have changed; it does not yet show how. Which channel dominates may depend on the state of the market. The question may be less which way is down than when the direction changes, and risk models should treat causality as a function of the regime.

Source: Showalter and Cho, HousingWire, Nov./Dec. 2008. Data as of Oct. 5, 2026.

Young Cho, Ph.D., is the Founder and CEO of PalmBridge Investment.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5533. Despite posting a solid earnings beat, Elastic sees its stock slide on rough guidance

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

The company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

However, investors were less than impressed with the company’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

Netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The company also sells application observability and security tools.

In the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the company has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

Elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) said he’s excited about the potential of those new capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”

Unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the company published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

Elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

#5532. The power of agile workflows

Mortgage lending workflows built on data triggers can reduce handoffs and rework. Agile queuing can lower cost per file touch while improving borrower feedback loops.   AI Summary

Every leader in this industry knows that every dollar matters, every teammate matters and every borrower matters. However, when we try to prioritize all of these, something often has to give. What if we didn’t have to compromise, though? What if it were possible to reduce costs, optimize your team and create a fast, easy borrower experience?

Agile workflows aren’t made of “unicorns and rainbows” and “all things possible” energy, but they are the answer to this.

Our industry’s cost of origination is at one of the highest points in history ($10,936 per loan as of Q2 2026). When approximately 70% of that cost is our operating overhead, how effective and efficient our teams are REALLY matters.

Today, most of our industry’s teams and technology operate around an extremely linear process that requires our borrowers to fit into our process that was designed to move paper. So, the borrowers that give you 100% of what you need on day one have the same process as the borrower who drags their feet and gets you what you need piece by piece.

We might be able to get one cleared to close a bit faster than the other, but both borrowers went from their loan officer to their processor, to an underwriter, back to a processor, back to the underwriter, then to closing. Every single one of those handoffs adds time, costs and frustration to the borrower who just wants to know if they are approved quickly and if they can close on time.

Agile workflows queue work to be completed when the data and documents say that the work can be completed. They don’t rely on milestones or handoffs.

For example, if a borrower has all of their income and employment documentation and data submitted but they haven’t found a property yet, that loan’s income and employment can still be queued for review by a decision maker (technology or an underwriter…it’s up to your organization’s risk threshold) who can issue that borrower’s income/employment approval, NOT pre-approval. We don’t have to wait until they find a property or until they go through processing.

Queuing work this way gives certainty to borrowers with a faster feedback loop. So, that borrower who brings everything in on day one finally gets rewarded for it. It also ensures that your team is only working on what matters most. They have work queued to them when it’s needed and the rest of their time can be spent building relationships with borrowers and referral partners.

That’s the borrower and team side. Now, let’s talk about cost. Every loan we originate has to meet very specific criteria from the GSEs or from private investors. So we can’t necessarily eliminate work that has to be completed, but we can eliminate handoffs, assign work to technology solutions, and reduce rework.

Let’s start here: Have you ever measured your cost per file touch? It’s your fulfillment cost divided by the total number of touches across your files. If you really want to dig into this even further, you can measure this by role type to see the cost of how many times your underwriter vs your closer vs your processor vs your AI agent touches the file.

I’m not suggesting we eliminate roles reviewing things when it’s needed, but I am saying that unnecessary reviews do cost an organization more than most of us realize.

Reducing unnecessary touches is critical, but that’s not really the power of agile workflows.  Agile workflows are the answer because they queue the right touches exactly when they’re needed to the exact right person on your team or the exact right technology that can complete the work on your behalf. It’s orchestrating the work between your team and your technology in a way that reduces friction while controlling risk.

This isn’t easy to operationalize, though. It requires three major shifts: building your workflow around data triggers instead of milestones, assigning decision authority by risk threshold of the work and measuring cost per file touch. Then, you have to align your team’s roles, expectations and incentive plans around these shifts.

This is A LOT, but it is possible with almost every LOS provider out there (including the one you’re likely already on), and the rewards are incredible for your team, your borrowers and your company.

I know we’ve been told that we have to choose between efficient teams, happy borrowers and our bottom line, but there is a better way. Agile workflows are the answer.

Melissa Langdale is chief executive officer and founder of Praxis Lending Solutions.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].
