#5531. Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for less than a third of its 2021 price

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The $3.68 billion deal is set to close in early 2027, after Mailchimp revenue fell 1% in Intuit's latest quarter

Intuit $INTU agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion, the company said on Thursday. The deal should wrap up in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

The price combines cash of $3.31 billion with Bending Spoons shares worth $368 million. That is less than a third of the $12 billion Intuit paid for Mailchimp in 2021, according to CNBC.

Intuit said it intends to use the cash proceeds to repurchase its own stock within fiscal 2027 after the deal closes. The company said the sale narrows its focus on AI-based tools that help businesses win customers, manage their sales pipelines and grow.

Mailchimp revenue slipped 1%, reaching $313 million, in the opening quarter of Intuit's fiscal year, which closed Oct. 31. For fiscal 2027, Intuit expects Mailchimp revenue of $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion, down 1% to flat. The company said its guidance excludes any impact from the sale and that it will update guidance when the deal closes.

The Mailchimp unit generated $1.3 billion in revenue for the fiscal year ending in July, roughly flat since 2024, according to Bloomberg. Bending Spoons purchases mature software businesses and restructures how they run in order to lift profits.

Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari $RACE said in an October interview that falling software valuations are creating acquisition opportunities for the company. Bending Spoons closed its Airtable acquisition in early September and struck a deal that month to buy Miro at a valuation of $1.36 billion. Its portfolio includes AOL, Vimeo, Evernote, WeTransfer and Eventbrite.

Berkshire Hathaway $BRK.B announced a $330 million investment in Bending Spoons on Oct. 14. On Oct. 27, Bending Spoons proposed a $1.5 billion offering of senior secured notes to fund acquisitions of other businesses.

#5530. Japan's ARK Signs MOU with U.S.-Based UMBC/IMET to Advance Grouper Hatchery Development

BALTIMORE, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ARK Inc. (ARK), a Japan-based aquaculture technology company developing modular recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) to make land-based fish farming more accessible, announced today that it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the University of Maryland Baltimore County (UMBC)Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology (IMET), a marine and environmental research institute based in Baltimore, Maryland, United States, to advance sustainable aquaculture.

Under the agreement, ARK and UMBC/IMET will collaborate on research, technology development, and demonstration activities related to grouper hatchery production in Baltimore, Maryland, leveraging ARK's recirculating aquaculture technology and IMET's aquaculture research expertise.

The collaboration will also explore the establishment of grouper hatchery facilities in Maryland, as well as opportunities for student training and workforce development aquatic resource conservation, and future commercialization. Both organizations will further examine the potential application of research outcomes in the United States, Japan, and other international markets.

The United States imports approximately 80% of the seafood it consumes, resulting in an annual seafood trade deficit of approximately USD 20 billion. In April 2025, a U.S. executive order aimed at strengthening the competitiveness of the domestic seafood industry highlighted the expansion of domestic aquaculture as a national priority.

Against this backdrop, ARK and IMET have been exchanging technical expertise and research insights to explore potential solutions to challenges facing the aquaculture industry.

In particular, the two organizations have been evaluating the potential application of ARK's modular recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) to support stable grouper hatchery production. Discussions have also focused on joint U.S.-Japan research into hatchery technologies and the potential development of the first commercial grouper hatchery in Maryland, United States.

The signing of this MOU marks a further step in these discussions, establishing a framework for cooperation in research, technology development, education, training and demonstration activities.

By combining ARK's aquaculture technology with IMET's aquaculture scientific expertise, the collaboration aims to advance grouper hatchery development in Maryland and the broader U.S. market, while exploring opportunities for future commercialization and international applications.

Under the MOU, ARK and UMBC/IMET will explore cooperation in the following areas:

Professor and Chair, Department of Marine Biotechnology and Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology (IMET), University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC)

"This MOU establishes a groundbreaking partnership between global aquaculture leaders at UMBC/IMET and in Japan to overcome critical bottlenecks in farming the grouper, one of the most heavily fished and high-demand marine species. By closing the grouper's life cycle and enabling year-round juvenile production, this initiative will make commercial hatchery-based grouper aquaculture viable. #5529. Hidden listings can keep serious buyers out, research suggests

The column draws on research in psychology, finance, and auction design to argue that limiting awareness can reduce participation and expected price. It advises agents to explain the scarcity versus obscurity distinction and to use broad reach with clear timelines when the seller goal is maximum price.  AI Summary

I have always taught that an agent’s listings are their store inventory. A shoe store with empty shelves does not sell shoes, no matter how friendly the staff is. For most of the year, the bulk of a listing agent’s energy should go toward building and protecting that inventory.

Which is why a question that came in for a recent coaching call deserves more attention than it usually gets. It was not about winning a listing. It was about keeping one.

An agent listed a condo and invested roughly $500 in photography and a virtual tour. The seller had an ongoing dispute with the homeowner’s association and had already spoken with an attorney. The agent knew all of this going in and believed it was settled. Then the association missed a response deadline, and the seller began talking about filing suit, and taking the property off the market.

The agent wanted to know two things. Was he going to have to give the listing back? And would he simply have to absorb the money?

What struck me about this question is how common the underlying gap is. Many agents work from listing agreements that address only the outcome everyone hopes for. The property sells, the transaction closes, the fee is paid. Very few agreements are explicit about the detours, and detours happen constantly.

Some withdrawals are completely sincere. A lawsuit, a family change, a decision to rent. Others are a polite way of ending the relationship so the seller can relist with another firm. From the agent’s side, the two can look identical. A well-constructed agreement does not need to tell them apart. It simply treats both fairly.

For brokers and team leaders, this is a systems question, not just an individual one. If your agents are each improvising in these moments, your company is losing money and listings in ways that never show up on a report.

The four scenarios every agreement should address

On the call, I walked through the provisions I believe belong in a listing agreement. Enforceability and wording vary by state, so have the specific language reviewed by a broker and a real estate attorney in your state.

1.​ Early cancellation. State clearly how and when either party can end the agreement before its term, and what is owed if that happens. Clarity in advance prevents arguments later.

2.​ Expense reimbursement. When the seller withdraws after the agent has paid for marketing, those documented costs are repaid by the seller. This is not a penalty. It keeps the agent from subsidizing a decision the seller made.

3.​ Rental conversion. If the owner chooses to rent during the term, the agent represents the rental on the same timeline. The agent built the relationship and the exposure, and that work should carry forward.

4.​ Conditional release. The property comes off the MLS, but the agreement remains in force for the balance of the term. If the owner sells or chooses to list again during that period, the original agent remains the agent of record or is still owed the fee, depending on how the agreement is structured.

Of the four, the conditional release is the one I find agents know least about, and it does the most work. It separates two things sellers tend to bundle together: removing a property from public marketing and ending a professional relationship.

When those are separated, the seller with a genuine reason gets exactly what they need, a quiet pause. The seller who was looking for a side door finds that the door is still connected to the original agreement. Either way, the agent’s investment and the relationship survive.

Agents sometimes worry these provisions will feel adversarial. In practice, a calm, plain explanation tends to land well.

Of course. Let us pull it from the MLS while you work through the association matter. The release will be conditional, which means that should you list again while our agreement is still running, we simply continue where we left off. Per our agreement, the photography and tour expenses are repaid, and if renting becomes the plan, I will represent the rental as well.

Most sellers respect structure. It tells them they hired someone who runs a real business.

Notice what is missing from that script. There is no argument, no guilt, and no attempt to talk the seller out of the decision. The agent acknowledges the seller’s reason, confirms the next step, and restates the terms that already exist. That sequence keeps the emotional temperature low, which matters, because a seller who leaves feeling respected is far more likely to come back, refer a friend, or call again when the association issue is resolved.

If you lead agents, review your standard listing agreement for these four scenarios this quarter. Then train your people to explain them at the listing appointment, not only when a seller is walking away. A provision the seller hears about for the first time during a withdrawal feels like a trap. The same provision introduced up front feels like professionalism.

A note on the buyer side as well. Agents representing buyers who know an association has a difficult or litigious history should share that with their clients, factually and with care. Protecting the client is the job on both sides of the table.

Agents who rebuild their inventory after every surprise withdrawal are always starting over. Agents whose agreements plan for every turn in the road keep their shelves stocked, season after season.

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

#5528. Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently launched AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business users. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.

#5527. Roaring Kitty's Mario post sends Nintendo stock higher

Free daily briefing on global business news.

GameStop stock also rose Thursday as the wider market fell, after the Roaring Kitty account posted an image of Cat Mario on X

Roaring Kitty, the online persona of investor Keith Gill, posted an image of Nintendo's Mario character on X $TWTR on Thursday, and Nintendo's American depositary receipts rose 3.2%.

The image showed Cat Mario, a form of the character that debuted in “Super Mario 3D World,” according to Bloomberg. The post carried no caption.

GameStop $GME stock rose 1.5% on Thursday, according to Bloomberg. The broader market declined, with all 11 S&P 500 sectors lower.

"Nothing else is working," Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak & Co., told Bloomberg. "The allocation to retail investors for Anthropic was small, so they're not benefiting much from that IPO. With all 11 S&P sectors in the red today, they're looking for anything they can sink their teeth into."

Gill first drew widespread attention in 2021's meme-stock episode, when his involvement helped send GameStop shares soaring, according to Bloomberg. He has made few posts on X since 2024, and several have moved stocks.

In May, GameStop and Chewy shares climbed after Gill's account put up and later removed an image of a cat, along with a second image showing Pepe the Frog in Roaring Kitty's red bandana, according to Bloomberg.

#5525. Netflix, Amazon, and Fox are expected to bid for 2030 World Cup U.S. rights as Disney sits out

Free daily briefing on global business news.

YouTube is expected to join the bidding for the U.S. rights, and FIFA plans to choose a winner before the end of the year

Netflix $NFLX, Amazon $AMZN, YouTube and Fox were widely anticipated to put in bids ahead of Thursday's cutoff for American rights to the 2030 men's World Cup, while Disney $DIS will stay out of the race, according to CNBC.

Fox and NBCUniversal's Telemundo hold the current rights, according to CNBC. FIFA would rather hand a single buyer the rights in both languages for the 2030 tournament, which Spain, Portugal and Morocco will host. Media companies can bid on the 2034 World Cup in Saudi Arabia as well.

Media executives expect the winning bid to land around $1.5 billion or higher, according to CNBC. The figure could differ if a single company ends up buying the rights to both the 2030 and 2034 tournaments.

Next week, FIFA executives intend to come to the U.S. to sit down with bidders, review their proposals and possibly gather final offers, according to CNBC. FIFA intends to pick the winning bidder prior to year's end. A FIFA spokesperson would not comment, saying the tender process is confidential.

Disney's ESPN spent recent weeks crunching its finances and found it could not afford $1.5 billion while also setting aside funds for its NHL, MLB, English Premier League and Champions League agreements, according to CNBC. Those deals will likely come up for renewal in 2027. ESPN weighed teaming up with another company on an offer but decided against it. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro had expressed interest in World Cup rights earlier this year.

NBCUniversal has not decided on a bid, which could put Telemundo's hold on the games at risk, according to CNBC. The company has already committed billions to the NBA and must also hold funds for MLB, perhaps the Premier League, and the NFL, whose talks are probably coming in 2028. Skydance and Apple $AAPL are sitting out.

Executives at media companies were budgeting between $1.5 billion and $2 billion per tournament for the 2030 and 2034 World Cups as of July. For the 2026 tournament, Fox paid $485 million for English-language rights and Telemundo paid $600 million for Spanish-language rights.

Netflix secured exclusive rights to stream all 104 matches of the 2030 World Cup in Spain and Andorra in October, the company said. Financial terms were not disclosed.

The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration yesterday, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible users to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform announced its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

These agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

#5521. Real Estate Expert Maggie Flartey-Kaminski Explains Key Factors That Matter When Selling a Home in the Poconos

Maggie Flartey-Kaminski examines pricing, presentation, timing, and buyer expectations within the Pocono real estate market.

POCONO LAKE, Pa., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should homeowners understand before selling a home in the Poconos? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Maggie Flartey-Kaminski of Century 21 of the Western Poconos in Pocono Lake, Pennsylvania, explains how sellers can better position their property within the unique Pocono real estate market.

According to the article, many buyers searching within the Pocono real estate market are not simply purchasing a house. Some buyers are seeking a vacation property for weekend retreats, while others are planning a long-term lifestyle transition centered around outdoor access and year-round living. The article notes that buyers often imagine how the property will support relaxation, family gatherings, and recreational activities before focusing on practical housing details alone.

Pricing strategy is another major factor discussed throughout the article. The article explains that properties appeal to different types of buyers depending on location, amenities, and intended use. Some homes attract vacation property buyers, while others are more appealing to full-time living arrangements. Pricing a home too aggressively can quickly reduce buyer interest, especially when buyers compare several similar listings during the same visit. The article notes that effective pricing should reflect both current market conditions and the lifestyle experience the property offers.

Photography and presentation also play a critical role when selling a home in the Poconos. Since many buyers begin searching online from outside the region, listing photos often create the first impression long before an in-person showing occurs. The article explains that images highlighting natural surroundings, fireplaces, outdoor recreation, lake access, and community amenities can help buyers better understand the experience the property provides. Strong presentation often helps create emotional connections early in the search process.

Seasonal timing can also influence buyer activity in the Pocono real estate market. According to the article, some buyers begin searching during ski season, while others become more active during warmer months when hiking trails, lakes, and outdoor spaces are easier to enjoy. Sellers who understand how weather patterns and tourism activity affect buyer behavior are often better positioned to time listings effectively and attract buyers whose priorities align with the property's features.

Community amenities receive additional attention throughout the article because they often carry greater importance than in many suburban markets. Buyers may evaluate lake privileges, ski access, clubhouses, hiking trails, pools, and short-term rental opportunities as carefully as they evaluate the home itself. The article explains that sellers who clearly communicate these lifestyle benefits often create stronger interest among buyers comparing multiple properties within the region.

Property maintenance is another issue buyers frequently evaluate in the Pocono market. The article explains that buyers may ask detailed questions involving snow removal, heating systems, storm preparation, and road access during winter conditions. Sellers who provide clear information about maintenance routines and seasonal care often help buyers feel more comfortable moving forward with the purchase process.

#5520. Industrial monitoring startup BrightAI closes $97M investment

BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, issues often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the company’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for issues that can’t be detected visually.

The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and  vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for  example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The company’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

The company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

“Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”

BrightAI says that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the company’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

#5519. I Built an AI Chatbot for $0. Here’s the Exact Stack.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

You don’t need money to ship a real, production-grade AI chatbot. You need to know which free tiers to stack. Here’s the exact toolchain.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I also built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot, and it cost me $0.

From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. Here’s the stack I actually used to build it layer by layer, what I did with each tool and what’s free about it.

Before writing a line of code, a chatbot needs a face. I used Figma to generate the chatbot’s logo straight from a text prompt describing the style and mood I wanted, then iterated on it a few times inside Figma itself rather than handing it to a designer. Figma’s own free plan covers individual use with unlimited file storage.

The whole project lives in a GitHub repository, private while the chatbot was still rough, and it’s the same repo both Claude and Codex connect to. GitHub’s free plan gives unlimited private repositories with a limited feature set and 2,000 minutes a month of Actions included on GitHub Free for standard runners on private repos, enough to run tests and basic automation without hitting a wall. Standard runners on public repositories stay free no matter how much you use them.

Claude Code did the actual building, the chatbot’s backend and the AI agents running inside it. I kept it connected directly to the GitHub repository and never let it touch the main branch directly: every task ran on its own branch, and nothing merged until I’d reviewed the diff myself and approved the pull request. The genuine free route in is a Guest Pass: if someone you know already pays for Claude Max, they can send you one, and it unlocks a full week of free Pro-level access.

I gave Codex a different job, connected to the same repository but never writing production code itself. It reviewed what Claude had actually shipped, acting as an independent judge on pull requests, and I also used it to draft the next development prompt I’d hand back to Claude, effectively having one model plan the work and another execute it. Codex has a genuine free plan at $0 a month. Free accounts run on GPT-5.6 Terra, OpenAI’s cost-efficient model for that tier. The free plan is capped at a usage limit rather than a time limit, which is exactly the size of job a reviewer role needs.

I bought the chatbot’s domain name through Cloudflare, where registration is usually cheap since Cloudflare sells at cost with no markup, and kept the DNS in the same place rather than splitting it across providers. From there I used Cloudflare’s free security layer to protect the domain, including rate limiting rules to stop any single source from hammering the chatbot’s endpoints. Cloudflare’s WAF documentation covers exactly this kind of rule, and the core protections, DNS, DDoS protection, and basic security features, are included on the free plan.

I used Railway for both the backend and the frontend, with a separate test environment so I could ship changes quickly without risking the live version. New accounts get a one-time free credit grant before any card is required, and unlike some free hosts, Railway doesn’t put your service to sleep by default the way its own documentation describes for its optional Serverless feature, so there’s no cold start tax on the free tier unless you turn that behavior on yourself.

Users sign up and log in through Clerk, and I built the whole flow using Clerk’s own test environment first, so I could try edge cases without creating real accounts or sending real emails. The free plan covers up to 50,000 monthly active users at no cost, which is more than enough room to move from testing into a real launch on the same setup.

Conversations, users and application data all sit in Neon, a serverless Postgres database that scales down to zero and stops costing anything the moment nobody’s using it. The free tier includes enough storage and monthly compute hours for a real early product, with no credit card required to start.

Once the chatbot’s AI agents were actually running, I needed to see what they were doing under the hood: which prompts fired, where they failed, and what they cost. Langfuse traces all of that, and its free Hobby plan includes a healthy monthly allowance of tracing events, enough to debug and monitor a real chatbot without paying anything.

I wired Exa and Firecrawl directly into the AI agents responsible for research inside the chatbot’s runtime, so the chatbot itself can decide when it needs to look something up. Exa handles the search, finding relevant pages for a given question, and its free tier hands new accounts starting credit plus a recurring monthly allowance with no payment method required. It also ships a playground where you can test a search query directly in the browser before wiring it into your agent. Firecrawl handles what comes next, turning a page Exa found into clean text the agent can actually read, and its own free plan includes a monthly credit allowance with no card needed either.

Before committing to a specific model for the chatbot’s agents, I used NVIDIA’s API Catalog to try several without paying per token. NVIDIA gives any developer free credits to test a wide range of hosted models through its own endpoints, which made it easy to compare options before locking in whichever one actually powers the chatbot in production.

The chatbot talks back, not just types, so I used Azure AI Speech for text to speech, letting the chatbot switch between a female or male neural voice depending on the setup. The free tier includes a real monthly allowance of neural voice characters at no cost, enough for genuine daily conversations before you’d ever see a bill.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I also built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot, and it cost me $0.

From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. Here’s the stack I actually used to build it layer by layer, what I did with each tool and what’s free about it.

Before writing a line of code, a chatbot needs a face. I used Figma to generate the chatbot’s logo straight from a text prompt describing the style and mood I wanted, then iterated on it a few times inside Figma itself rather than handing it to a designer. Figma’s own free plan covers individual use with unlimited file storage.

#5518. BJ's Wholesale Club is raising its full-year earnings forecast after a strong quarter

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The warehouse club operator lifted its adjusted EPS range to $5.10 to $5.30 as third-quarter comparable club sales rose 13.5%

BJ's Wholesale Club raised its full-year adjusted earnings forecast on Friday, setting a new range of $5.10 to $5.30 per share versus $4.60 to $4.80 previously. The company moved the bottom of its guidance for comparable club sales growth, not counting gasoline, up to 2.5% from 2%. The high end stays at 3%.

Adjusted earnings for the third quarter ended Oct. 31 were $1.73 a share, compared with $1.16 a year earlier. Net income rose to $219.5 million from $152.1 million, and total revenues rose 17.5% to $6.28 billion.

Analysts were forecasting a quarterly adjusted profit of $1.26 per share on revenue of $5.97 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Comparable club sales rose 13.5% in the quarter, or 4.1% excluding gasoline sales. Membership fee income increased 9.5% to $138.4 million. Digitally enabled comparable sales grew 38%.

"We delivered a strong third quarter driven by robust traffic growth and record membership," Chairman and CEO Bob Eddy said in a statement. Chief Financial Officer Laura Felice said, "we are raising our full-year guidance for both comparable sales and adjusted EPS."

Merchandise gross margin rate, which excludes gasoline sales and membership fee income, fell about 170 basis points from a year earlier. The company attributed the decline to promotions tied to its 42nd birthday celebration event.

Selling, general and administrative expenses dropped to $696.1 million from $788.2 million a year earlier. They included a benefit of about $240 million, net of legal fees, from a settlement of litigation over credit card interchange fees in which BJ's was the plaintiff. The company recognized an estimated $95 million in expenses tied to the use of the settlement proceeds, which partly offset the benefit. Gains from sale-leaseback transactions also lowered expenses, while labor, occupancy and operating costs rose with new club and gas station openings.

Operating income rose 43.7% to $313.8 million.

For the fiscal year ending Jan. 30, 2027, BJ's expects capital expenditures of about $800 million. The spending supports new club openings and upgrades across its distribution network, including the ambient distribution center.

BJ's opened two new clubs and five gas stations in the quarter. It operates 271 clubs and 211 gas locations in 22 states.

The company scheduled a conference call on the results for 8:30 a.m. ET on Friday.

#5517. Etherscan Warns of Support System Access Attempts as Security Scares Hit Crypto and Banks

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In…

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal users’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

#5515. Lawmakers form bipartisan caucus to create meaningful AI safety legislation

A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers said today they’re forming a new AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

The lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks. They also pointed to another incident involving the now-public Anthropic PBC, which also reported that its agents escaped their testing environments to access third-party systems.

These incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” said Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems and threats to national security.”

Whitesides (pictured) is co-chairing the caucus alongside Representatives Nathanial Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia). In a post on X, they stressed the need for bipartisan collaboration to create the basic policy guardrails for AI safety, citing the growing concerns of the American public.

Does it feel like there's a new tech or AI crisis every day? Recent headlines are raising serious concerns about our digital safety and security.

Today, I'm joining @RepDonBeyer, @RepNateMoran, and over 20 of our colleagues to launch the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation… pic.twitter.com/bhMyygy1J6

— Rep. George Whitesides (@Rep_Whitesides) November 19, 2026

The 26-member caucus includes seven Republicans, which is a surprising number given that the White House administration under President Donald Trump has strongly opposed any heavy-handed regulation of the AI industry. The goal of the caucus is to identify “targeted solutions” that ensure AI remains under control without derailing innovation and threatening America’s lead in the industry.

Whitesides said the lawmakers will focus on two things: proposing legislation to augment AI safety, and responding quickly to high-profile security incidents by gathering developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and come up with solutions.

“We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides told Politico in an interview. He said the group will work together to propose, provide feedback and endorse new AI legislation. He believes there’s an urgent need for this, because most other groups within the House are more focused on educating members or creating legislation within their own parties, he said.

Another thing the caucus intends to do is to pursue relationships with outside AI experts who can help lawmakers to navigate complex policy decisions. It also wants to help raise public awareness around AI and its safety issues, and ensure members outside of relevant committees have the tools they need to contribute to new legislation and debate.

In the recent midterm elections, Americans made it clear that AI is becoming a major issue for governance. Moreover, a recent survey revealed that 43% of Americans don’t trust either of the two major political parties to properly get a grip on AI safety, according to a one-pager that accompanied the press release.

“Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue,” Moran said. “This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared.”

#5514. Anthropic’s $81 Billion IPO Is the Biggest Ever — Here’s Who’s Getting Rich and Who Missed Out

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude is now a $2 trillion public company. Not everyone is happy.

Anthropic, the company behind the popular AI chatbot, surged more than 30% in its Nasdaq debut today after the largest IPO in history. It sold more than 980 million shares at $83 apiece for $81.3 billion, topping the then-record $75 billion SpaceX raised in June, according to The New York Times. Shares opened at $111.50 under the ticker “ANT,” valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion.

The biggest winners of the Anthropic IPO are the company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, president Daniela Amodei. Each holds a stake that could be worth $20 billion or more, according to the Times. On the VC side, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Iconiq hold stakes worth more than $25 billion at the IPO price, The Wall Street Journal reports. Menlo Ventures’ stake is worth roughly $22.5 billion. Amazon, Google and Gulf sovereign wealth funds are also in line for huge paydays.

Then there’s Sam Bankman-Fried. The FTX founder led Anthropic’s $580 million Series B in 2022. After FTX collapsed, its bankruptcy estate sold the $500 million stake in 2024 for about $1.3 billion. At the IPO price, those shares would be worth roughly $37 billion today. China was also locked out of the offering.

#5513. Ubisoft stock drops 11% as GTA VI competition dims its holiday forecast

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Assassin's Creed maker expects about €250 million in net bookings for the quarter ending in December and kept its full-year targets

Ubisoft forecast net bookings of about €250 million ($280 million) for the quarter ending in December, and its stock fell about 11% in Paris trading on Friday.

The company said on Thursday that the outlook reflects a crowded holiday season. Ubisoft confirmed its full-year targets: net bookings down by a high single-digit percentage, a high single-digit negative non-IFRS operating margin and free cash flow consumption of no more than €500 million ($560 million).

The €250 million forecast is a 26% decline from €338 million a year earlier, according to Bloomberg. The forecast falls short of the €361 million analyst consensus that TD Cowen pointed to, according to Reuters. Reuters also said the outlook reflects a thinner slate of content releases than is normal.

Ubisoft stock fell to €3.72 after dropping as much as 15% during the session, and it is down 42% this year.

Rockstar Games, a label of Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, launched “Grand Theft Auto VI” on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S, with the U.S. release on Thursday. The game earned a Metacritic score of 99. Ubisoft’s holiday-quarter titles will compete with it, according to Bloomberg. The game is believed to have taken in $2 billion on its opening day, according to Reuters.

Ubisoft’s second-quarter net bookings were €389 million, above its guidance of around €370 million. The company credited “Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced” for the outperformance. Second-quarter net bookings were down 20.8% from €490.8 million a year earlier.

For the first half of the fiscal year, net bookings were €644.7 million, down 16.5% from a year earlier. Ubisoft posted an IFRS operating loss of €189.2 million, compared with a loss of €120.2 million a year earlier. Headcount fell by close to 1,100 over the six months, and the fixed cost base was €660 million, down 6%.

Ubisoft said the second half of its fiscal year will benefit from the releases of “Rayman Legends Retold” and “Just Dance: Decades of Hits,” along with continued “Black Flag Resynced” sales and a stronger fourth quarter for “Rainbow Six Siege.”

The company expects a stronger content pipeline in fiscal 2027-28 and 2028-29. It expects to return to free cash flow generation and positive non-IFRS operating income in fiscal 2027-28.

#5511. Gap is cutting its full-year forecast as Banana Republic and Athleta stumble

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Gap cut its net sales outlook to "roughly flat" from growth of 1% to 1.5% as warm weather weighed on demand

Gap $GPS lowered its full-year outlook on Thursday after warmer weather weakened demand in October and early November, the company said.

The owner of Old Navy, Gap, Banana Republic and Athleta expects fiscal 2026 net sales to be "roughly flat," down from a prior forecast of growth of 1% to 1.5%. Adjusted earnings per share are projected at $2.29 to $2.34, compared with a prior range of $2.35 to $2.45. Adjusted operating margin is projected at 7.2%, down from a prior range of 7.4% to 7.6%. For the fourth quarter, Gap expects net sales to be flat to down 1%.

Gap said the outlook reflects a slower start to the fourth quarter, followed by improvement as weather normalized. The company furnished the earnings release to the Securities and Exchange Commission in a Form 8-K filing.

"While demand softened in October and early November, amidst warmer weather, we are encouraged by the more recent improvement in trends as temperatures have cooled," CEO Richard Dickson said in a statement.

Third-quarter net sales rose 2% to $4.0 billion, and comparable sales were flat. Net income was $311 million, or 86 cents per share, up from $236 million, or 62 cents per share, a year earlier. Analysts had expected comparable sales to rise 1.3%, according to CNBC.

Banana Republic comparable sales fell 3%, which Gap tied to shoppers' reaction to its women's fall assortment and to customers postponing purchases of heavier seasonal clothing. Athleta comparable sales fell 15%, a drop the company blamed on its attempts to refresh the product lineup and marketing, which gained little momentum with shoppers. Old Navy comparable sales were flat, while Gap brand comparable sales rose 9%, the 12th consecutive quarter of growth.

Dickson told CNBC that much of the lower guidance stemmed from warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter. He said the company anticipates "meaningful acceleration" as shoppers head into the busiest stretch of the holidays, according to CNBC.

Gap named Ashley Kechter, a Vuori executive, as Athleta's next president and CEO. She starts Dec. 14, according to CNBC. "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. Kechter will head a wide-ranging assessment of the brand, Dickson said.

Banana Republic stocked too heavily in sweaters and outerwear, according to Bloomberg. Michael Francis began as Old Navy's CEO on Nov. 2, according to CNBC.

Gap stock was up as high as 4.3% before the opening bell on Friday. As of Thursday's close, the stock was down 27% for the year.

#5510. Canada’s sovereign AI ambitions come with a local economic bargain

Data center backlash is pushing builders to show communities what they get in return, and public-private partnerships are becoming one answer. As the race for sovereign AI heats up, the question is shifting from where intellectual property lives to where compute runs and who profits from it.

Canada offers a sharp test case. A modern data hall employs few people, but its profits can fund the startups and jobs a region needs, according to Sharif Virani (pictured), chief executive officer of SPUR Innovation Center.

“There’s a big misnomer right now in the world that’s kind of landing from previous tech, where people think where your IP is where the wealth creation is going to be,” he said. “It’s not the case anymore. You have to make sure your inference happens in your country or in your region.”

Virani spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed sovereign AI, reinvesting data center profits in local entrepreneurs and winning over residents through public-private partnerships. (* Disclosure below.)

SPUR treats its Waterloo, Ontario, site as an innovation campus with an attached data hall rather than a pure data center. The company reinvests about 10 percent of the campus’s data center profits in local entrepreneurs through a venture studio and takes first right of refusal on their office space and compute, Virani explained. Canada’s Dominion List counts more than 500 founders who have left for San Francisco, he noted.

“We have entrepreneurship at an all-time low, productivity at an all-time low [and] GDP in freefall,” he said. “That’s really the result. We’ve got to reverse that.”

One of SPUR’s early investments went to two international students who had full scholarships to the University of Toronto and internships lined up in San Francisco. Instead, they launched a startup called Auditorium AI and hired staff, according to Virani. The model also reaches Main Street, where on-campus hackathons helped a former long-haul trucker build AI software for logistics.

“AI allows these people who know the problem, who have earned the right to solve the problem, to mobilize technology to do it and make the lives of their friends, families and neighbors better,” Virani said.

#5508. More Than 20,000 Small Businesses Use His Technology. Here’s His Data-Driven Advice—And AI Shortcuts—for Capitalizing On a $1 Trillion Holiday Season.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Andrew Stern, co-founder and CEO of Quilt Software, breaks down the success strategies.

The holiday shopping season is in full swing — and it started early this year.

New data from specialized point-of-sale software company Quilt Software, which serves more than 20,000 independent retailers, from jewelers and pet stores to liquor stores and grocers, showed a 7.6% same-store sales growth spike in October year over year.

That’s in stark contrast to the Q1 through Q3 2.7% to 3.2% bump, which might largely be attributed to inflation, Quilt Software co-founder and CEO Andrew Stern tells Entrepreneur.

What’s more, customers aren’t just getting a head start; they’re also making more frequent shopping trips. Year-over-year transactions per store grew 6% in Q3 and 7.9% in October, per Quilt’s data.

This year, Small Business Saturday, which saw an estimated $18 billion in spending at independent retailers in 2025, falls on November 28, just 27 days before Christmas.

With customers opting for earlier and more frequent purchasing, independent retailers that want to make the most of the limited window need to stay on top of which items are selling in real time to remain ahead of trends and maintain inventory, Stern notes.

The CEO also cautions independent shops against attempting to compete with big-box retailers like Amazon or Walmart on price or convenience, calling it a “race to the bottom.”

Instead, Stern suggests a two-pronged approach for independent retailers: Lean into what makes them special, and use AI in a way that works for them (it won’t look like it does for mega-retailers).

“ For our small independent merchants, they opened their store for a reason,” Stern says. “They thought they were bringing something really unique that no one else had. So lean into that, because you’re probably right.”

One in five holiday shoppers plan to purchase gifts and other holiday items at small or local businesses this year, according to the National Retail Federation’s (NRF) October Holiday Consumer survey.

Shoppers planning to buy from small businesses cited reasons including supporting the community (71%), seeking unique gifts and décor (56%), championing artists through handmade purchases (37%) and finding high-quality products (33%), per the report.

It’s clear that holiday shoppers want what independent retailers have to offer — but it’s crucial that those stores put themselves on people’s radar.

“ Make sure that [customers] can see you, that you’re visible when people do their Google searches, or increasingly their ChatGPT searches,” Stern says. “Make sure that you come up because they want to find you.”

Nowadays, independent retailers must have an answer engine optimization (AEO) strategy to stay relevant and show up in search results. Earlier this month, Entrepreneur spoke with Courtney Sandora, founder of digital marketing agency Go Social, to learn more about how brands can compete in the AEO landscape.

Sandora notes that customers use LLM-powered search engines to ask specific questions, so savvy businesses should hone in on the queries they can reliably and successfully own, “seeding” stories and copy that bolster their authority.

“That storytelling extends across everything from PR to creators, even how you appear on a retailer website,” Sandora says. “Typically, on retailer websites, there’s a short description. Is the message you want to tell in that retailer website description? Consistency matters.”

It’s critical that small businesses use rapidly advancing AI technologies to their advantage.

However, that won’t look exactly like it does for major retailers, which might harness AI to manage six-month supply chains or optimize warehouse logistics, Stern says.

Instead, independent retailers should focus on taking small steps with significant impact, like using agentic solutions to outsource specific tasks they might not have time to execute to their fullest potential.

For example, the right AI tool can give shop owners the marketing support they’ve never had, unfolding in the background as they help customers at the counter. Quilt offers its retailers an AI marketing assistant that can create campaigns for customers with their own inventory.

“ This generative AI is able to create copy that’s in their voice,” Stern says, “that’s tailored to different cohorts of customers and can say, ‘Hey, come in, I think we have some products that you might be interested in. Here they are.’”

Quilt also offers an AI assistant that can help small retailers navigate unwieldy piles of inventory.

Stern points to thrift stores, which tend to rely on volunteer staff to sift through large amounts of donations quickly, as an example. Shops can snap a picture of a leather couch and receive a price estimate immediately.

The AI tool can also help them identify rare and valuable items that might otherwise go unnoticed. “ We’ve had some crazy cases like, ‘Oh, that looks like a Tiffany lamp. Look at the bottom of it and see if there’s a signature that says Tiffany. If so, do not charge $5 for that lamp,’” Stern says.

The NRF expects retail sales in November and December to grow 4.2% over 2025, for a total spending surpassing $1 trillion. That’s a massive opportunity for independent retailers that opt out of competition with big-box retailers and leverage the data to win their share.

That’s in stark contrast to the Q1 through Q3 2.7% to 3.2% bump, which might largely be attributed to inflation, Quilt Software co-founder and CEO Andrew Stern tells Entrepreneur.

#5507. Procter & Gamble is cutting up to 30% of its supply-chain jobs by 2030

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The company plans a 20% to 30% cut in its product-supply workforce, contractors included, and targets $1.8 billion in annual savings

Procter & Gamble $PG said at its investor day on Thursday that it plans to shrink its product-supply workforce by 20% to 30%, including contractors, by 2030.

P&G listed the reduction alongside two other commitments for 2030: $1.8 billion in productivity savings and free cash flow productivity of 90% or more. Chief Product Supply Officer Luc Reynaert presented the commitments.

The cuts are part of Supply 3.0, the company's supply-chain program. The program aims to hold supply steady, bring more digital and automated processes into operations, teach workers to use the new tools and make operations more sustainable, according to The Wall Street Journal.

P&G is aiming for as much as $10 billion in total productivity savings. The target spans the period from fiscal 2027 to fiscal 2030, and the $1.8 billion falls within it, drawn from the cost of goods sold, according to Reuters. CFO Andre Schulten said the savings are intended chiefly to fund reinvestment.

P&G has opened 15 "unattended" logistics sites and intends to add more over the next few years, according to Bloomberg. Reynaert said the operations should help productivity climb 20% by 2030, "freeing up our employees for higher value work."

About 52,000 employees spread across roughly 35 countries worked in manufacturing as of a May 2025 filing, close to half of P&G's headcount, according to Bloomberg.

P&G announced a portfolio and productivity plan in June 2025 and expects about $2 billion in before-tax restructuring costs over two years. The company said last year that 7,000 corporate roles would be eliminated across a two-year span as part of the plan, according to Bloomberg.

P&G cautioned last month that higher costs for raw materials, energy and freight would squeeze annual profit further, according to Reuters. P&G stock gained 1.2% before the opening bell on Friday.

#5505. Enterprise AI hits a wall of power and cooling, not GPU supply

Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

Those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

“When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan said. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”

Hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

The economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

“Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan said. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”

SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the company builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent New Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

“You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan said. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”

Busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the company’s AI and Cyber Lab.

“It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan said.

#5504. FAA is set to reveal the cause of the router outage that halted U.S. flights

Free daily briefing on global business news.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will brief the public on the findings

Federal Aviation Administration chief Bryan Bedford said Thursday that officials plan to disclose by the end of the week what caused the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop, which stemmed from a router outage, according to Reuters.

Bedford would not talk about what investigators had found, according to Reuters. He said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would be the one to present the outcome to the public. The disruption hit over 18,000 flights and 1 million travelers.

The FAA said it issued the ground stop at about 3:30 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 after a technical problem, and air traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m. that day. Instability hit 17 of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The agency said its legacy equipment became unstable when data flooded the network at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.

The FAA said its initial investigation points to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas. L3Harris, the FAA's network service provider, had been working at the El Dorado site, including deploying a new router. The agency said it has no indication of a cyberattack and that it and L3Harris continue to investigate the root cause. Operators canceled approximately 12,462 flights on Nov. 13, though not all cancellations were directly caused by the ground stop, the FAA said.

Duffy has blamed the ground stop on a Juniper router that L3Harris put in at a remote facility in Arkansas, according to Reuters. He said the earlier rollout of 68 routers from Juniper Networks $JNPR, a unit of Hewlett Packard Enterprise, caused no trouble. The FAA said it disabled the router function involved at the originating routers and more than 60 others, and has paused installing them.

Testing is ongoing at L3Harris’ Florida lab, where personnel from the FAA, Cisco $CSCO and the FBI are present, according to Reuters. A Hewlett Packard Enterprise spokesperson said the hardware performed the way it had been set up, according to CNN.

Earlier this week, Duffy said officials had not determined whether contractor error or a faulty router caused the flood of data. Bedford said the router replacement was routine maintenance of the existing telecommunications network and not part of the $12.5 billion air traffic control modernization effort.

Bedford said the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, which L3Harris has operated since 2002, needs replacement, according to Reuters. "We have a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network, which is why we've got to get off of it as fast as humanly possible while maintaining safety," Bedford said.

#5503. M&A Isn’t Just for Big Companies. Here’s How Startups Can Do It With No Cash.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Most entrepreneurs don’t realize there is another way to grow their business: through mergers and acquistions.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Most startups are so focused on building stand-alone businesses through traditional sales and marketing that they overlook other ways to grow, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A).  They simply have not been trained on the topic and don’t know that, for some businesses, it can be a faster, more effective way to scale.

This article will provide a high-level tutorial on what M&A is, why you should consider it, and how to negotiate deals that can get to the finish line, even if you are not large enough to be bankable.

A merger is a combination of the shareholders of two businesses into one. A merger typically involves combining the management teams and operations into one.  An acquisition is exactly what it sounds like: your business is acquiring a company (or being acquired by one), with the acquiring team retaining 100% control over all key decisions in the new company. The acquired company’s operations will be integrated into the new company, however the acquiring company sees fit, as the buying company will control all decisions post-transaction. So, you will need to decide which scenario will work best for your needs.

M&A has many advantages, the key ones being speed, economies of scale and removing competition. Since the acquired business is already up and running and, hopefully, producing cash flow, it offers a much faster path to growth. For example, if a restaurant chain was trying to grow from 1 to 2 locations, it would take them over a year to find a site and build it out. But through M&A, that second location is already built and is immediately generating revenues today.

Furthermore, when you combine two businesses, you can eliminate duplicative costs and achieve economies of scale. For example, you don’t need two executive teams, two insurance policies, two marketing agencies, two accounting firms, etc. By removing these duplicative costs, the combined business will end up with a more profitable bottom-line margin, where hopefully 1+1=3.

As for the competitive advantages, by buying a competitor in the market, that will increase your market share and have you competing against one less competitor (which may help your pricing).  As an example, in my hometown of Cary, NC, one entrepreneur acquired and rolled up around 20 competing Mexican restaurants, with the goal of ensuring that no matter which Mexican restaurant you ate at, he was getting the sale, with nearly 100% market share.

That all said, things can go wrong with M&A.  Be sure to read my prior article on the potential pitfalls with M&A, so you don’t get into any trouble here, and you go into this M&A direction “eyes wide open” to prepare for potential hurdles that may arise in the future.

Depending on the size of the transaction, M&A can be funded either from the buyer’s cash account, or by raising additional capital from investors, or with no cash at all via an exchange of equity between the two businesses. Since most start-ups don’t generate much profit, it is unlikely they will be bankable. So, this last path of exchanging equity makes it possible for companies of any size to pursue M&A without any financing required at all.

The key thing about M&A is that it does not necessarily need to be dependent on economic or financial market conditions. Even if third-party investors have paused new investments during a down market, nothing prevents two businesses from merging in a cashless transaction at any time. So, if you can’t raise capital for your stand-alone restaurant chain growth, you can still be growing using M&A as the driver of that growth.

For established businesses generating revenue and profits, it is pretty easy to value those companies using historical revenue or profit multiples from past transactions in your industry. For example, if most small restaurants are sold at 3x EBITDA, it is reasonable to assume your small restaurant can be valued at 3x EBITDA. A good business broker can advise you on what the normal multipliers will be for the size of your company’s revenues, profits, and growth rate.

If you don’t have revenues or profits to value, then you need to use another metric.  Maybe that is cash invested in the business, or asset value, or the assets themselves.  For example, if one real estate owner has 4 locations and another real estate owner has 2 locations, then perhaps those two businesses could be combined into one business where the 4-location business owned 67% and the 2-location business owned 33% of the new company.

Let’s say two self-storage businesses are exploring a merger. One does $6MM in revenue, $1MM in profit, and has 300,000 square feet of buildings (all mature, open for many years). The other has $2MM in revenue, $0 in profit today (but will end up at $1MM after they fully rent out their space) and also has 300,000 square feet of buildings (but they are brand new still ramping up clients and revenues).

How do you value this? On revenues, it would be 80/20. On profits, it would be 100/0, and on square footage it would be 50/50. If I were the buyer, I would start the ownership at 75/25, and if the smaller business successfully increases its client base per its plan, it can earn its way up to 50/50 through an earn-out. That seems to be the fairest for all parties; that should get both parties to the finish line.

I am a former investment banker on Wall Street, and M&A is incorporated into my DNA. It is something I am comfortable with, as I have bought and sold many companies over my entrepreneurial career. But if you are a first-timer here, I know it can be “scary.”  But it doesn’t need to be. Surround yourself with smart M&A advisors who have “been there and done that,” both in terms of negotiating M&A and integrating companies post M&A, and everything should turn out just fine.

And hopefully your shareholders will thank you for materially accelerating your growth and helping them to expand their valuation multipliers as a bigger company. Good luck!

Most startups are so focused on building stand-alone businesses through traditional sales and marketing that they overlook other ways to grow, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A).  They simply have not been trained on the topic and don’t know that, for some businesses, it can be a faster, more effective way to scale.

This article will provide a high-level tutorial on what M&A is, why you should consider it, and how to negotiate deals that can get to the finish line, even if you are not large enough to be bankable.

A merger is a combination of the shareholders of two businesses into one. A merger typically involves combining the management teams and operations into one.  An acquisition is exactly what it sounds like: your business is acquiring a company (or being acquired by one), with the acquiring team retaining 100% control over all key decisions in the new company. The acquired company’s operations will be integrated into the new company, however the acquiring company sees fit, as the buying company will control all decisions post-transaction. So, you will need to decide which scenario will work best for your needs.

#5502. Sky Protocol Shows Resilience Through Record $2 Billion Day as Review Finds CoinDesk Report Misleading

Over $2B exchanged through the PSM with USDS holding 1:1 throughout. A transaction-level review by Block Analitica finds that CoinDesk's report on the Peg Stability Module contains several critical misleading statements, and covers under 0.06% of PSM's ~$960B volume.

GRAND CAYMAN, Cayman Islands, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Sky Protocol reports that users exchanged more than $2 billion of USDS for USDC through the Peg Stability Module (PSM) on November 19, marking one of the largest single days of outflows from the PSM to date. The PSM continued to operate as designed, with USDS exchanged for USDC at 1:1 throughout, and the USDC in the PSM did not fall below $800 million before rising above $1.1 billion today. According to financial.skyeco.com, the collateral in the Sky Protocol, about $9.3 billion in total, exceeded the USDS and DAI in circulation throughout.
