#5501. Chicago Fed president won't rule out a larger rate hike for December

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Austan Goolsbee said how steep the path of rate increases needs to be depends on what inflation does, after months of high readings

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee did not rule out a larger interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, according to Bloomberg.

Goolsbee took part in a moderated Q&A at the Economic Club of Indiana luncheon in Indianapolis on Thursday, according to the Chicago Fed.

"We've now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress," Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday, according to Bloomberg. "So everything's always on the table, in my view, and how steep that path needs to be is determined by what we think is happening with inflation."

Goolsbee said he is concerned about seasonal factors. Inflation has been running hot during a stretch of the calendar that usually brings cooler prices, he said, and upward price pressure has typically been strongest early in the year. That makes it "that much more relevant that as we roll into next year, do we think that the through line is going to be another jump back up in the inflation rate?" he said, according to Bloomberg.

He said officials had expected the price effects of tariffs and costlier energy to fade sooner than they have. He described the construction of infrastructure that runs artificial intelligence as a "second component, which to me looks like the beginnings of just ordinary demand overheating."

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said again on Wednesday that policymakers could need to weigh a half-point hike in December, according to Bloomberg. Minutes of the October meeting, released Wednesday, show another unidentified official joined Waller in calling for that discussion. Goolsbee is not a voting member of the policy committee this year, but he will be next year.

Goolsbee called the October consumer price report "borderline disturbing" in an interview last week. Asked then about a bigger hike in December, he said he would rather not box in policymakers before they meet. The consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, and core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3%.

Waller said in a London speech last week that a half-point increase should be considered if October core CPI came in around 0.3% or higher. The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September and held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% in October. Its next meeting is Dec. 8-9.

Inflation rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier by the Fed's preferred gauge. Core CPI has come in above expectations for three consecutive months, according to Bloomberg.

#5500. I’ve Been a CFO, a CPA, a Franchisee and a CEO — Here Are the Credentials That Get You Hired Now

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I’ve worked in a variety of roles, but credentials follow you from job to job. Check out the credentials that get you hired.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

Early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Big 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

Each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

I see this play out every week. As a franchise consultant, I spend most of my time with directors, vice presidents and CXOs, many of them facing a restructuring. Their resumes are stacked. Yet the ones who land on their feet fastest, whether that means a new role, a board seat or a franchise award, rarely win on titles. They win on a different set of credentials, and some of those can be built in months, not decades.

A title says you held a job. A point of view shows how you thought while you held it. When I was a CFO at a real estate developer, my work was buried in spreadsheets and board meetings. Nobody outside the building knew how I approached the cash crunch during the Great Recession or difficult acquisitions.

When I started my national consulting firm, I had no choice but to put my thinking in public. I began posting regularly on LinkedIn about franchise ownership, career transitions and the lessons learned as a franchisee. That consistency, more than any credential on my profile, is why strangers started calling. More than 20,000 people now follow me, and many executives tell me they read my posts long before reaching out to me.

Pick two or three topics where your experience gives you a unique viewpoint and write about them every week. You aren’t building an audience for its own sake. You’re creating a searchable record of your expertise.

Earlier in my career, my network was mostly people I’d worked with directly. That works until you’re in transition or need help outside your industry, which is exactly when most people need it. I learned this through three reorganizations. Three of the four companies I worked for over 26 years no longer exist. So I started nurturing my network long before I needed it.

Franchisors taught me this lesson from the other side of the table. When candidates apply to buy a franchise, the franchisor evaluates them just as carefully as the candidate evaluates the brand. The candidates who move through smoothly are the ones other people will vouch for — former colleagues, bankers and existing owners in the system.

This is where LinkedIn Premium has earned a spot in my toolkit. I use Sales Navigator to find and follow the executives I serve and to identify mutual connections who could make a warm introduction. I don’t use it to blast messages. I use it to find a valued connection who can vouch for me, and then I ask that person directly.

Think of 25 people who will take your call tomorrow. If fewer than half of them work outside your current company, start widening the circle now, while you don’t need favors. And never send a message that doesn’t offer the other person something of value.

This credential surprises executives the most. As a CEO, I had people build the model, chase the receivables and fix the website. As a fitness franchise owner, I was the OEO — the Only Executive Officer — and I tell my candidates to expect the same.

Hiring managers and franchisors are asking a version of the same question: Will this person roll up their sleeves and do the work, not just direct it? You answer that with evidence. Maybe you’ve run a side project, advised a small business or built your own department or systems.

Today I run a national practice largely on my own. The tools I pay for earn their keep only because they let one person do the work a small team used to do.

Identify one hands-on accomplishment from the past two years that didn’t depend on a team and make it visible.

The fastest way to look obsolete is to describe how things were done a decade ago. The old adage “if it isn’t broken, don’t fix it” doesn’t apply today. The executives I see winning today are adaptable. One of my candidates just bought a second franchise in a different industry because she has an insatiable appetite for learning.

After more than 30 years in business, I’m still learning. I’m working on a second edition of my book because some of my original advice needs updating. Admitting that isn’t a weakness. It tells people I’m paying attention.

Be ready to explain, in two sentences, something you’ve learned in the past six months and how you’ve applied it. I’m not dismissing traditional credentials. My CPA background is the reason candidates trust me to walk them through financing options. My years as a CFO and CEO gave me pattern recognition no course could teach.

But titles are only a starting point. They tell people what you’ve done. The four points above tell them what you’ll do next.

Start this week. Write one post that shares a real lesson from your career. Reach out to three people outside your company. Add something to your profile that you built, not just something you managed. Those small moves compound faster than you’d expect.

If you want a head start, LinkedIn’s Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to find the ones that fit the way you work.

I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

Early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Big 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

Each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

#5499. SpaceX sold $32 billion in AI chip debt, with most at yields above 8%

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The sale is part of a more than $40 billion financing that funds Nvidia chips SpaceX will lease for about five years

SpaceX sold $32 billion of debt tied to Nvidia $NVDA chips on Thursday, with most of it priced at yields above 8%, according to Bloomberg. The debt was sold in three parts and will fund the company's access to AI chips.

The largest piece was Class A3 notes totaling roughly $25.2 billion, which were priced to yield 8.259%, according to Bloomberg. The average yield on U.S. investment-grade bonds is 5.95%, according to Bloomberg index data. Roughly $6 billion of the A3 notes was bought by institutional buyers on Thursday, while earlier placements accounted for the remainder.

The money will pay for Nvidia chips bought by Saturn Funding Trust, a special-purpose vehicle managed by an Apollo Global Management entity, according to Bloomberg. SpaceX will rent the hardware under a lease lasting roughly five years. The deal is structured so the debt stays off SpaceX's books, and it forms one piece of a financing worth over $40 billion that additionally involves bank loans.

Goldman Sachs $GS and Apollo ran the transaction, according to Bloomberg. Spokespeople for the firms and SpaceX did not reply when Bloomberg asked for comment.

Saturn Funding Trust purchases the chips, yet SpaceX remains obligated to keep paying on the lease if the hardware breaks down or a force majeure event such as a natural disaster strikes, according to Bloomberg. The structure should allow SpaceX to hold on to its investment-grade credit ratings.

The debt package will cover roughly $47.3 billion in GPU equipment, primarily the newest Rubin chips from Nvidia, according to Bloomberg. Delivery is expected to start in January. Accounts at BlackRock $BLK, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR numbered among the cornerstone buyers.

Davis Hebert, head of technology, media and telecom at CreditSights, said the pricing was deliberately generous so that more conventional buyers would take part, according to Bloomberg. He said clients have been skeptical of the deal after losses on SpaceX's unsecured bonds earlier this year.

Those bonds were part of a $25 billion high-grade offering priced days after SpaceX’s initial public offering in June, which raised $86.2 billion including the underwriters’ option, according to Bloomberg.

SpaceX is not the only AI company turning to chip-backed financing. CoreWeave was seeking an investment-grade loan of at least $4 billion last week, backed by chips and related contracts. Early discussions pointed to a yield of 7% to 7.5%.

#5498. Ross Stores stock plunges after cutting its profit forecast on higher fuel costs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Ross Stores raised its full-year earnings forecast to $8.75 to $8.84 a share while it trimmed its fourth-quarter outlook

Ross Stores $ROST lowered its fourth-quarter profit forecast on Thursday, and its stock dropped as much as 12% in extended trading.

The off-price retailer reported third-quarter results and said it expects fourth-quarter earnings per share of $2.16 to $2.25, or growth of 8% to 13%. The prior range was $2.17 to $2.26. The new range falls below the $2.27 analysts expected, according to Bloomberg.

Higher fuel costs drove the reduction, with added spending on holiday staffing and advertising also contributing, Chief Financial Officer Bill Sheehan told analysts on a call, according to Bloomberg.

Ross Stores kept its fourth-quarter outlook for comparable store sales growth of 4% to 5%, on top of a 9% gain last year. The company raised its fiscal 2026 earnings forecast to $8.75 to $8.84 a share. That range includes a benefit of about 60 cents a share from refunds of tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, recognized in the second quarter.

For the third quarter ended Oct. 31, sales rose 12% to $6.3 billion from $5.6 billion a year earlier. Comparable store sales rose 8%, on top of a 7% gain last year. Net income was $606 million, compared with $512 million a year earlier, and earnings per share were $1.91, compared with $1.58. The company had guided for earnings of $1.75 to $1.83 a share.

Operating margin was 12.3%, up 70 basis points from a year earlier and above the company's plan of 11.7% to 12.0%.

"Customer traffic remained the primary driver of our comparable store sales growth," CEO Jim Conroy said in a statement.

Sales peaked at the start of the period, when shoppers hunting for back-to-school bargains filled the aisles, while weather that ran warmer than forecast dampened demand as autumn went on, Conroy said on the call, according to Bloomberg.

Ross Stores opened 51 stores in the quarter, completing its 2026 plan of 115 new locations. Ross Stores stock was up 22% for the year as of Thursday's close.

XRP currently has 63.5 billion tokens in circulation. At $100 per token, its market capitalization would reach $6.35 trillion. That would put XRP among the most valuable financial assets in the world, exceeding the market capitalization of most publicly traded companies.

The bullish argument rests on XRP’s potential to capture a much larger share of institutional payments, cross-border settlements, and digital asset liquidity. A stronger crypto market could also provide the liquidity needed for another substantial XRP rally. But XRP would need considerably more capital, adoption, and sustained demand to justify a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

The historical comparison remains fascinating. XRP went from less than a penny when GTA V launched to several dollars during subsequent crypto cycles. Few people back then would have believed XRP could get to where it is now.

#5496. If Your Business Can’t Run Without You, You Have a Bigger Problem Than You Think

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Being indispensable might feel like success, but it can quietly limit your company’s growth.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

A client needs an update. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

One lesson I’ve learned is that being needed and being effective are not always the same thing. And for entrepreneurs, recognizing that difference can change how a company grows.

In the beginning, founders have to do almost everything.

You win the business, manage customers, handle finances and solve problems because there isn’t anyone else. You know where everything stands. You remember the commitments you’ve made. You understand why certain decisions were taken.

That knowledge becomes an advantage. But as your company grows, it can also become a problem.

Employees get accustomed to asking you because you know the answer. Customers prefer speaking directly with you because you’ve always been available. And gradually, even decisions that should be made elsewhere find their way back to your desk.

The strange part is that this can feel rewarding. Being the person everyone needs reinforces the belief that you’re essential to the company’s success.

But ask yourself something uncomfortable: If the business requires your involvement in nearly every decision, have you actually built an organization, or have you simply created a more demanding job?

I’ve seen business owners respond to overwhelming workloads by hiring additional employees. Sometimes that’s exactly what the business needs. But adding people doesn’t automatically reduce the founder’s workload.

If nobody has the authority to make decisions, additional employees may simply create additional questions. I previously explored this problem in an Entrepreneur article about examining workflows before hiring.

The underlying issue is often less about headcount and more about how work moves through an organization.

Consider a project manager who is responsible for delivering a client project but needs the founder’s approval for every minor adjustment. Technically, the project has been delegated. In reality, the founder is still managing it.

The project manager has responsibility without sufficient authority, and that creates frustration on both sides. Delegation only works when people know which decisions they can make independently, what boundaries apply and when something genuinely needs to be escalated.

This is the part of leadership that requires some self-reflection. It’s easy to complain that employees keep asking questions. It’s harder to recognize that our own behavior may have encouraged it.

If a manager makes a reasonable decision and we immediately reverse it, we’re teaching that person to seek approval next time. If we insist on reviewing every email, presentation and customer response, we’re communicating that we don’t trust others to exercise judgment. And if we consistently step in to solve problems before employees have a chance to work through them, we’re reinforcing the very dependency we want to eliminate.

I’ve learned that people need room to make decisions, including decisions that may not be exactly the ones I would have made. That doesn’t mean lowering standards. It means being clear about the result you expect while allowing capable employees to determine how to achieve it.

A team doesn’t become independent because the founder announces that everyone should take more ownership. Independence develops when people are genuinely given the opportunity to exercise it.

One aspect of running a business that doesn’t receive enough attention is the mental burden of keeping everything moving.

You may delegate the preparation of a report, but still be the person remembering when it’s due. You may assign someone to manage a client, but still feel responsible for anticipating every issue that could arise. You may have a team handling operations while remaining the person mentally tracking every unresolved problem.

The work has been distributed, but the responsibility hasn’t. This distinction reminds me of the concept of the mental load, often discussed in the context of family responsibilities and working mothers.

The same principle applies to leadership. There’s a difference between completing a task and being responsible for remembering, organizing and following through on everything associated with it.

If a founder continues carrying all of that responsibility, delegation may provide temporary relief without changing the underlying problem. True ownership means someone else is accountable for both the task and the outcome.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to run a simple experiment.

Choose five business days when you deliberately step away from routine operational decisions. You don’t need to disappear completely. Remain available for genuine emergencies and decisions involving significant financial, legal or reputational risk. But resist the temptation to intervene in every ordinary problem.

Before the experiment begins, clarify who owns each function and what decisions they can make. Then pay attention to what happens.

Do projects continue moving? Can customers get answers? Are managers comfortable making decisions? Where does work stall? More importantly, why?

Perhaps employees lack access to information. Maybe approval limits are unclear. Or perhaps certain processes exist only in your head. Those are the issues worth fixing.

When the five days are over, review the decisions your team handled successfully alongside the problems they encountered.

Don’t use the exercise to identify who failed. Use it to understand where the business remains unnecessarily dependent on you.

Entrepreneurs often associate growth with more customers, higher revenue and larger teams. Those are important measures.

But I would add another: How much can your business accomplish without requiring the founder to supervise every detail?

This doesn’t mean becoming disconnected from your company. A founder should remain closely involved in strategy, major relationships and decisions that shape the future of the business. But there’s a difference between leading an organization and personally keeping every part of it functioning.

As you plan the next stage of growth, look beyond what your business is accomplishing and examine how it’s accomplishing it.

Are you developing leaders who can make sound decisions? Have you created processes that survive someone’s absence? Can your team solve problems without waiting for you? If not, you may have a business that’s growing in size without growing in capability.

Here’s the challenge I’d leave every entrepreneur with: Take five working days away from routine decisions and see what breaks.

Whatever stops working deserves your attention when you return. Because the goal of building a business shouldn’t be to make yourself indispensable forever. It should be to build something strong enough that you don’t have to be.

There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

A client needs an update. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

#5495. The entrepreneurship scorecard is broken. We’re measuring the wrong things.

Pratham Mittal is the founder of Tetr College of Business. The student-venture figures in this piece come from Tetr’s own cohorts.

Business schools have become remarkably good at telling stories about entrepreneurial success. We count companies launched, capital raised, revenue generated and founders who go on to build something meaningful. These numbers make for compelling headlines and impressive institutional scorecards. But they leave out a more consequential question: what happens when the business doesn’t work?

At Tetr College of Business, we have had a front-row seat to both sides of this experience. Our students have built businesses, taken products to market, acquired customers, managed costs and, in some cases, discovered that their original assumptions did not hold up. When we examined the outcomes across our cohorts, what stood out was not simply how much revenue students had generated, but the considerable variation in what they had built, what they had earned and what they had lost.

That distinction matters because entrepreneurship is rarely a linear progression from idea to success. It is an exercise in navigating uncertainty, making decisions with incomplete information and constantly reconciling ambition with the realities of the market. If we are serious about preparing people to build businesses, we must be equally interested in understanding the ventures that struggle as we are in celebrating those that succeed.

Across 59 student-built drop shipping businesses, our cohorts generated more than $172,000 in reported revenue, with an overall reported profit margin of 21.86%. At first glance, these are encouraging numbers. But the individual businesses reveal a more nuanced picture of what it takes to make an idea commercially viable.

The scale of these ventures varied considerably, as did the economics behind them. Bike Arena, a student-led venture dealing in new, demo and pre-owned performance bicycles, emerged as the largest by revenue, recording $102,361 and a profit margin of 21.98%. Tafflo, which focused on technology accessories, generated $18,008 in revenue and a 63.64% profit margin.

Smaller ventures also demonstrated different levels of commercial performance. Juvak, a gaming accessories brand, recorded $2,396 in revenue at a profit margin of 53.21%. Claycia, which offers a curated range of bags, from travel bags to everyday totes, generated $5,342 in revenue, with a 12.47% margin.

The contrast is instructive. A business generating six figures in revenue is not necessarily more economically sound than one generating a few thousand dollars. Revenue tells us whether customers are buying; profitability reveals how much the business retains after accounting for costs. Neither, however, tells us on its own whether the business can sustain itself over time.

Our direct-to-consumer ventures offered another illustration. In the Class of 2028, 21 student-founded brands generated $186,862 in reported revenue, with an average reported profit margin of 30.62%. Ikrara, a silverware and jewellery brand, contributed $120,210 in revenue, with a 16.99% margin. Knotcultured, a premium streetwear venture, generated $11,460 but reported a considerably higher margin of 61.78%.

One demonstrated the ability to generate demand at scale; the other retained a greater proportion of its sales as profit. Both are meaningful outcomes, but they point to different aspects of building a business. Understanding that distinction is as important as learning how to generate the first sale.

The picture becomes more revealing when we look beyond the stronger performers.

Elantherm, a venture developing wearable period-relief belts with heat and massage functions, generated $1,906 in revenue but recorded a loss of $900. Welz Company, which sold smart rings, generated $2,491 in revenue and recorded a loss of $369 in the team-level records. Several other ventures in a subsequent cohort reported no revenue in the available reporting period. One team pivoted at the last minute, leaving insufficient information to assess its eventual commercial outcome.

It would be easy to leave these businesses out of the story. But doing so would give us an incomplete understanding of what students actually experienced.

A product can be developed, a website launched and a marketing campaign executed, yet the economics may still not work. Sales do not automatically translate into profit. A product that appears promising to its creators may struggle to find customers willing to pay for it. And even when demand exists, the cost of acquiring and serving those customers can make the business difficult to sustain.

The more important question is what founders do with this information. Do they revisit their pricing? Rethink their distribution strategy? Reconsider the customer they are trying to reach? Or recognise that the original idea needs to change altogether?

We should not assume that every loss has the same explanation. But learning to interrogate the numbers rather than explain them away is an essential part of building a business. The ability to recognise when an assumption is wrong, and the judgement to change course, can be as consequential as the conviction to pursue an idea in the first place.

Our Kickstarter projects offered another perspective on this process. Seventeen student teams launched live campaigns, collectively raising $79,532 from more than 1,100 backers, against a combined funding target of $75,000.

Some campaigns significantly exceeded expectations. Taowist, a glow-in-the-dark playing-card product, raised $12,032 against its target, reaching 1,475% of its goal. SlidePass, a smart passport wallet, raised $7,849, reaching 430%. Others fell short. ClickBuddy reached 67% of its funding target, while Brett reached 80%.

The distinction matters because Kickstarter operates on an all-or-nothing funding model: campaigns that do not meet their goals do not receive the pledged funds. For these students, the exercise was not simply about presenting an idea convincingly. It was about discovering whether people who had no obligation to support them were willing to put their money behind it.

That is a very different experience from receiving feedback on a business plan in a classroom. The market does not respond to the amount of effort invested in an idea or the elegance of its presentation. It responds to whether a product solves a problem, whether the price makes sense and whether the value is compelling enough for someone to pay for it.

This is where entrepreneurial education needs to evolve. Students should not only learn how to identify opportunities; they should have the opportunity to test their assumptions against actual customer behaviour, understand the consequences and make decisions based on what the market tells them.

There is a larger implication here for business education. If we evaluate entrepreneurial programmes primarily through the number of ventures launched, revenue generated or funding raised, we risk presenting an incomplete picture of what it means to build a business. We may also create an incentive to celebrate outcomes without examining the decisions that produced them.

The business world rarely offers the certainty of a well-structured case study. Markets shift, customer preferences change, costs rise and strategies that look convincing on paper encounter realities their founders did not anticipate. The ability to navigate these moments, interpret what is happening and make decisions with incomplete information is what separates an interesting idea from an enduring business.

Business schools must reflect that reality in how they teach and measure entrepreneurship. Alongside revenue and funding, we should pay attention to profitability, customer acquisition economics, capital efficiency, product-market fit and the ability to recognise when a business model needs to change. Equally, we must be willing to examine the ventures that did not work, rather than allowing their stories to disappear from the institutional record.

And this is an evolving story. A new wave of student ventures is already taking shape at Tetr College, with teams building SaaS businesses in the US, launching Kickstarter campaigns in China and developing direct-to-consumer brands in India. These ventures will bring a different set of ideas, markets and challenges to the table. Their outcomes are yet to be seen, but that is precisely the point: entrepreneurship is an ongoing process of testing, learning and building, not a collection of success stories captured at a single moment.

I do not believe every student should graduate with a successful company. That would be an unrealistic expectation and, more importantly, the wrong measure of what an education should achieve. The objective is not to turn everyone into a founder, but to ensure that every student develops the ability to recognise opportunities, make decisions with incomplete information and adapt when circumstances change. The discipline to follow the numbers, the confidence to act on evidence and the willingness to question one’s own assumptions are skills that extend well beyond starting a business.

The next generation will enter a world where uncertainty is the norm. A founder whose venture does not work may find themselves building a career within a startup or a large technology company. The ability to learn, unlearn and relearn – to make sense of unfamiliar situations, solve problems and find a way forward – is what will allow them to navigate that transition. These capabilities matter just as much to someone entering the workforce as they do to someone building a company. They make people more adaptable, resourceful and self-reliant, less dependent on any one role, organisation or economic cycle to define their next step.

Ultimately, entrepreneurship cannot be taught by celebrating only the businesses that make it. We must also examine those that struggle, understand where the assumptions fell short and learn what could be done differently. The real measure of entrepreneurial education is not simply how many businesses students build, but whether they leave better equipped to build, adapt and find their footing in an uncertain world.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Anthropic received about $91.6 billion of the proceeds, and a concurrent $26.0 billion private placement lifts the total to $119.5 billion

Anthropic closed its initial public offering with gross proceeds of about $93.5 billion after its underwriters exercised in full their option to buy additional Class A common stock, the company said on Friday.

The offering priced at $83 per share. Before underwriting discounts, commissions and other expenses, Anthropic received about $91.6 billion of the proceeds. The company said it received nothing from stock sold by selling stockholders.

The company said the IPO and the private placement together brought in about $119.5 billion before deductions.

Anthropic's Class A stock began trading on the Nasdaq $NDAQ Global Select Market on Thursday under the symbol "ANT." The stock slid by over 10% in the hours before Friday's opening bell.

The underwriters' overallotment option is known as a greenshoe, according to CNBC. The $93.5 billion total surpasses the amount raised in SpaceX's record IPO in June.

Goldman Sachs $GS and Morgan Stanley $MS were lead book-running managers for the offering. The company said a registration statement became effective on Nov. 18 and that the offering was made only by means of a prospectus.

Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday in the largest IPO on record. The stock opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, 17% above the IPO price. The major U.S. averages each dropped more than 2% that day.

#5493. Current price of oil as of November 20, 2026

At 7:15 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $92.83 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s a drop of 58 cents compared with yesterday morning and more than $29 higher than the price one year ago.

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5492. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5491. How the Race to Control Product Recommendations Is Changing the Creator Economy

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Reddit’s new ad test points to a bigger shift: Platforms are connecting creators, communities, AI discovery and shopping to influence the decision before a customer buys.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

What does a Reddit search ad have to do with the creator economy? More than it first appears. When someone looks up a gaming headset or asks which software is worth paying for, Reddit wants to be more than the place where people discuss the options. It is testing ads alongside search results, putting promotions close to a high-intent decision.

That move makes more sense when you look at the conversations Reddit is selling access to. The company points advertisers to its 1,300 gaming communities and cites TransUnion research finding that 71% of U.S. Reddit gamers had purchased a gaming product based on information they found on the platform.

It is a platform-sponsored finding, not a forecast for every campaign. Still, it shows why community context can be more valuable than a broad audience count: The discussion may already be helping someone decide.

Reddit is building out that decision path inside its product. In a test, AI-powered product discovery can summarize community discussions, show product information and send shoppers to a retailer. A user could ask for recommendations, compare what Redditors say and move toward a product without starting over somewhere else.

There is a business reason to make that journey shorter. Reddit’s ad revenue climbed 54% in the third quarter of 2026. Yet the company also faces a vulnerability: In October, its CEO said search referrals fell by more than a million a week on average, citing changes to Google’s AI search experience. Building a destination people use directly is one way to reduce reliance on another company’s results page.

Reddit’s AI strategy has another side. The platform has given Google structured access to Reddit content and formed a partnership with OpenAI, while developing its own AI search and shopping tools. Those moves create a tension: The same discussions can help answer a question in another product, attract an ad on Reddit or lead to a product listing on Reddit. Who gets the value from that recommendation is becoming a business question, not just a product question.

The pattern extends well beyond Reddit. On YouTube, creator partnerships and shopping connect brand discovery, sponsored videos, product tags and affiliate income. Pinterest is making it easier for creators to connect storefronts to product pins. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode, bringing sponsored offers into conversational search. Each company starts with a different strength, whether it is video, visual inspiration, search or community. All are trying to connect influence to action with fewer steps in between.

This is a bigger definition of the creator economy. It includes the creator, but also the system around that person: discovery tools that match a brand to a voice, paid distribution that extends a post’s reach, shopping features that monetize a recommendation and AI that helps a customer make sense of it. Communities can play a similar role even when there is no single influencer at the center.

For brands, a shorter path from recommendation to purchase can make campaigns easier to run and measure. The trade-off is that a platform may control the audience data, the recommendation, the ad placement and the definition of success. Creators face a similar bargain. New tools can open income streams, but access depends on platform rules, algorithms and fees. And the communities whose conversations influence a purchase may not share in the value those conversations create.

I have seen this kind of shift before. Search began as another channel to test; the companies that moved early understood it was infrastructure for existing demand. Discovery is changing again. People can use AI search and Google during the same research process, then look for a creator’s review or a community’s experience. That overlap makes it harder to assign one channel all the credit, but it does not make each influence less important.

For a brand, the competition is often for the moment before purchase, when someone decides which options deserve a closer look. The platform that earns that moment can shape the shortlist long before a customer reaches a checkout page.

Begin with the facts an AI assistant, creator or customer might use to describe your business. Product details, pricing, availability, policies and differentiators should be accurate wherever they appear. Strong third-party coverage, credible reviews and useful customer experiences give people evidence to evaluate. A paid placement cannot compensate for conflicting claims or stale information.

Then plan around context, not just audience size. A creator’s expertise or a community’s product knowledge may matter most when someone is comparing options. Paid media, communications, creator partnerships, search and ecommerce teams should be working from the same view of that journey.

Measurement needs the same broader lens. Track AI mentions, branded searches, qualified leads and sales alongside creator and community activity. Ask customers what helped them decide. Platform reporting is useful, but compare it with your own results instead of assuming a view or click tells the whole story. Building AI search visibility is part of that work, not a substitute for measuring whether the right customers act.

Finally, give people a reason to keep the relationship going beyond the platform: useful product information, a strong site experience, an email program or a customer community. The goal is not to avoid platform commerce. It is to benefit from the new routes to discovery without making one company the only place your brand can be found, understood or purchased.

Platforms are turning recommendations into a product. Brands that recognize the shift can earn a place in the decision, while keeping enough independence to understand what is working and why.

What does a Reddit search ad have to do with the creator economy? More than it first appears. When someone looks up a gaming headset or asks which software is worth paying for, Reddit wants to be more than the place where people discuss the options. It is testing ads alongside search results, putting promotions close to a high-intent decision.

That move makes more sense when you look at the conversations Reddit is selling access to. The company points advertisers to its 1,300 gaming communities and cites TransUnion research finding that 71% of U.S. Reddit gamers had purchased a gaming product based on information they found on the platform.

It is a platform-sponsored finding, not a forecast for every campaign. Still, it shows why community context can be more valuable than a broad audience count: The discussion may already be helping someone decide.

#5490. AI shopping tools are steering consumers toward unfamiliar retailers, Norton warns

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Gen's Norton says 42% of Americans plan to use a tool like ChatGPT for holiday shopping as fake shop activity rises 129%

Norton, a unit of Gen, warned in its 2026 holiday scams report that AI shopping assistants are steering more shoppers to unfamiliar retailers, while scammers use AI to build fake online stores.

The company released the report Nov. 5. It said 63% of Americans surveyed have used an AI shopping assistant or agent, and 83% would use one. Of those who would, 42% are confident the assistant would recognize and avoid a fraudulent website.

Of the respondents with experience using an AI shopping assistant or agent, 56% reported that the tool had suggested or completed a purchase from a retailer they were unfamiliar with, according to CNBC.

Gen Threat Labs has seen AI assistants miss scams, the company said. In one case, a shopper asked an assistant for affordable alternatives to a designer leather jacket. The recommendations included a $279 jacket from a fraudulent online store, listed beside legitimate retailers with no warning. Norton said shoppers may trust a recommendation because it comes from AI, even when the site behind it cannot be trusted.

Gen Threat Labs data shows a 129% increase in fake shop activity compared with the start of last year's holiday season. The Gen family of brands, including Norton, blocked nearly 25 million attempted visits to fraudulent shopping sites in the last month, the company said. The number of fake store domains blocked doubled from 260,000 in the 2024 holiday quarter to 526,000 in 2025.

Leyla Bilge, Norton’s global head of scam research, said AI’s biggest effect on scams has come through coding, which lets scammers put up “thousands and thousands of fake e-shops online,” she told CNBC. That makes any given shopper more likely to land on one.

"Scammers are counting on holiday shoppers being rushed, distracted and afraid of missing out," Bilge said in a statement.

Norton's survey of 1,000 U.S. adults, conducted by Dynata from Sept. 10 to Sept. 21, found that 16% have been scammed while holiday shopping online. Among the victims, 88% lost money, and the average amount lost came to $394. A further 35% said they had made a purchase from a site or seller they suspected could be a scam, tempted by a deal that seemed too good to pass up.

Norton advises shoppers to vet any retailer an AI assistant suggests before confirming a purchase. It also recommends going straight to the retailer's website or app instead of clicking a social media ad, and paying by credit card or a payment service with buyer protection.

Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, said shoppers cannot assume an AI suggestion has been checked for legitimacy. "You absolutely need to check with the retailer directly," he told CNBC.

#5489. Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development

Tencent and Alibaba said this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S. restrictions on access to advanced AI processors, yet acknowledged that they could still slow the development of new AI models.

Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S. Department of Commerce released an interim rule expanding export controls on Monday, making them some of the first Chinese corporate responses to the restrictions.

Chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule also requires a license for large data centers to offer substantial computing power to Chinese customers. Together, the measures are likely to restrict the amount of computing power available to Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent as they develop AI models and offer them to users.

Tencent executives, in the company’s earnings call, drew a distinction between the computing power needed to train new models and running existing ones.

“We actually don’t see an impact because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” James Mitchell, Tencent’s chief strategy officer, told analysts on Wednesday. (Inference is the running of AI models, as opposed to training them.)

Mitchell added that Tencent had reached a stage where the inference could run on what he called a “surprisingly limited number” of domestically produced chips.

Martin Lau, Tencent’s president, agreed that the domestic supply chain should be able to cover inference, particularly for Tencent’s smaller, more efficient models.

Still, Lau called the restrictions “unfortunate” and admitted that it would now take longer for Tencent to train the next version of its Hunyuan model. “It sets everyone back in China,” he said.

In the long run, Lau predicted that U.S. controls would “speed up” the development of China’s domestic chip industry. “We believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips.”

Tencent reported 207.3 billion yuan ($31 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-on-year. Fintech and business services revenue, which includes cloud computing, rose 9.4% to reach 63.6 billion yuan ($9.5 billion).

Net profit rose 0.3% to 65.1 billion yuan ($9.8 billion). Capital expenditure rose 527% to 81.4 billion yuan ($12.2 billion).

On Thursday, on its earnings call, Alibaba said its 2030 targets—including $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin—remain on track despite the new restrictions.

“Our own progress in developing domestic computing power is in fact already ahead of our original expectations,” Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu told analysts on the call. The company has invested heavily in its in-house chip division, T-Head, which it plans to list in Hong Kong.

Alibaba reported 271.5 billion yuan ($40.5 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 10% year-on-year. AI and cloud revenue rose 53% to reach 61.0 billion yuan ($9.1 billion).

Net profit also rose by 213% year-on-year to 64.4 billion yuan ($9.6 billion). Capital expenditure rose by 60% to reach 50.5 billion yuan ($7.5 billion).

Alibaba’s confidence in its longer-term targets came with a warning about the near term.

“The new compute export control rules will affect next year’s products and services, and there is still uncertainty as regards the supply chain,” Wu said during the earnings call. He suggested that cloud revenue growth could slow to between 30% and 45%, then rebound to 50% or higher by 2028.

Wu said it was “too early at this stage” to know how U.S. restrictions might affect the development of its Qwen family of models, though he added that the company’s current T-Head chips “are already capable of fully supporting the training of large-scale, including ultra-large-scale, models.” Wu predicted that T-Head production would ramp up in 2027 or 2028. “Once we get there, we will actually be in a better position to control and pace the speed at which we iterate our foundation models,” he said.

Alibaba, however, is in the spotlight after the Nvidia scandal, which toppled CEO Jensen Huang last week. Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, before U.S. chip export controls took effect in 2022, the Information reported. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, is suspected of funneling advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls; Megaspeed denies the allegations.

On Thursday, a group of Alibaba shareholders sued the company, accusing it of concealing its ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. The shareholders said media reports of the ties contributed to a 14% drop in Alibaba’s share price over four days, and accused it of understating the risk that export-control violations could harm its business.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Commerce Department faces increased scrutiny over whether it has done enough to keep advanced chips out of China. On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released data showing the department had approved nearly 880,000 AI chips for Chinese companies—including 75,000 for Alibaba and 150,000 for Tencent—out of more than 3.4 million chips that Nvidia and AMD sought to export to Chinese companies.

Chinese AI developers beyond Tencent and Alibaba are preparing for the likely impact of tighter U.S. chip restrictions. The Information reported Thursday that Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, had scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia’s Blackwell chips through an Indonesian data center.

The new controls also constrain the ability of Chinese companies to manufacture their own semiconductors using overseas foundries. New U.S. rules narrow the exemptions that chip manufacturers can use to ship advanced chips without a license. The Financial Times reports that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Samsung Electronics have suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers.

#5488. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5487. Anthropic is now AI’s bellwether

For months, I’ve been on high Anthropic alert. I suspect many of you have, too.

Waiting for the S-1 to drop for months, I’d often have conversations that ended with “who knows, tomorrow might be the day.” I was even mildly anxious going off to my cousin’s wedding, beset by nightmares of the S-1 coming out while I was on the dance floor. And yesterday, watching Anthropic (a company that’s only about five-years-old) close on the Nasdaq to the tune of a valuation of $1.27 trillion (or $1.76 trillion, depending on how you calculate it), it occurred to me: Finally, AI has entered its “show me the money, for real” era.

“An Anthropic IPO marks a major milestone for the AI industry, but it will also fundamentally reset the bar for startups,” said Woodson Martin, CEO at low-code development platform OutSystems, via email. “Under public-market scrutiny, inference costs, capital efficiency, and unit economics will matter just as much as the technology itself. With greater visibility into frontier lab economics, investors will demand proof that smaller players have durable moats.”

Anthropic will face more questions than ever: The model maker’s first day of trading was positive but mixed, as shares soared initially to a peak valuation above $2 trillion before dropping and eventually closing up about 17%. Alone, this means zilch, but the broader backdrop was uneasy: As Anthropic traded for the first time, the market bristled with volatility, ultimately with the Nasdaq down 2.25% and the Dow down 2.19% at close.

Anthropic is now a first-of-its-kind public company, with a business model that simply didn’t exist at the beginning of this decade. And this company’s untested AI-era business model—which includes Claude Code usage, subscriptions, and enterprise deals—is now a matter of public record and is financially susceptible to public sentiment.

A risk, certainly, given Anthropic’s prominence in the “AI could kill us all” narrative. That accountability is by-design, said Ravi Mhatre, cofounder and managing director at Lightspeed, which has backed Anthropic since 2023 and led the company’s Series E with the firm’s largest-ever single check.

“Anthropic going public is really about this coming-of-age,” Mhatre told me. “It marks an important milestone for artificial intelligence that it’s powerfully capable, being run in a company that adheres to public standards, and that implies something about transparency… It implies something about the ability for society to participate as stakeholders in the company.”

Set to cash out over the coming months, Mhatre and Lightspeed are among Anthropic’s big-ticket VC backers (though, per PitchBook, the company has over 400 venture backers and no VC has an over 5% stake). The same’s true of Iconiq, which invested over $6 billion in Anthropic and had a roughly 2% stake in the company’s last round, a source familiar with the matter confirmed. Will Griffith, Iconiq partner and Anthropic backer, pointed out to me just how impossible Anthropic’s trajectory would have been mere years ago.

“This is completely unprecedented in terms of a company… founded less than six years ago, achieving this scale and this level of impact,” said Griffith. “This is totally unique in history and something that the markets and the world have never seen before.”

I always hesitate to call anything unprecedented, since very few things are truly, historically unprecedented. However, as a practical matter, Griffith is entirely correct: No company in history has ever gone from zero to a trillion-dollar public company in under six years, until now. But (especially in the AI era) just because a company is massive, that doesn’t mean it’s mature. Nevertheless, Anthropic is now AI’s official weather vane.

“Anthropic is an important and critical bellwether of the AI ecosystem,” said Joe Fath, partner at VC firm Eclipse, via email. “There’s outsized importance that it trades well in the public markets to support the ‘AI trade.’”

From here, AI will be iterating on its economics in the bright, unforgiving light of the public markets. To my mind, it’s about time.

#5486. Trump fired White House cyber director, tapped Pentagon official as replacement

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will serve as acting national cyber director after Sean Cairncross's exit

US President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC on July 14, 2025. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images)

President Donald Trump is replacing White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross with Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, who will take over in an acting capacity, according to CNN. Administration officials confirmed the change on social media on Thursday, and a White House official told CNN that Cairncross is leaving the administration.

Cairncross was fired, according to CBS News. A source in the White House told CNN that Trump "fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position as he lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job."

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pushed for the change, according to Axios. Two sources described the departure as amicable.

Cairncross said in a statement to CNN that he is "incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence." He has held the post since August 2025, according to CBS News.

Davies thanked Trump, Miller and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a social media post on Thursday, according to CNN. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come ... but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on,” she wrote. Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated her.

The Office of the National Cyber Director is responsible for coordinating strategy and policy on cybersecurity throughout the federal government. A permanent director must receive a nomination from Trump and approval from the Senate, according to CNBC. The Senate will be run by Democrats starting in January, which leaves little time to put forward a nominee, according to CBS News.

Davies already won Senate approval to serve as chief information officer at the Defense Department, according to Axios. She advises Hegseth on information technology and cybersecurity. Prior to entering government, she held a position at Unilever, where she oversaw cyber resilience efforts worldwide.

The change follows a run of U.S. technology outages that the administration has attributed to patching and system upgrades. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Rubio, who is also national security adviser, said the administration sees no indication of a coordinated cyberattack or state-sponsored activity behind the incidents.

The outages include a halt to flights across the country, a worldwide Microsoft $MSFT Outlook failure and, reportedly, a blackout of the classified communications network used by the National Security Agency, according to CNBC. Democrats have objected to how the administration has handled the situation, according to CNN.
