#5485. SEO Isn’t Over, But Google Is Losing Its Monopoly. Here’s How to Adapt.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The shift from traditional search to AI-powered discovery is changing the future of digital marketing.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Like clockwork, the digital marketing echo chamber sounds the death knell every few years: “SEO is dead.”

I entered this game in the early 2000s as a web developer. I was building sites at night while working a full-time job during the day. If I wanted traffic, I had to figure out search engine optimization through trial and error.

My first transactional store lived on Yahoo! Stores, selling generic mini MP3 players — that is, until the iPod wiped that category out overnight. Next, I sold GPS navigation software on CDs, which stopped when the iPhone made standalone navigation devices obsolete.

Then came an ecommerce brand called Soccer Nation. Growth happened fast. We opened a physical storefront in Vista, California, at the same time that David Beckham signed with the LA Galaxy of the MLS, and watched revenue climb for years. Then the 2008 recession froze retail spending. We shuttered the retail shop and sold the domain to a competitor who turned it into an online soccer publication.

This is important because I’ve spent more than two decades watching technological and economic disruptions dismantle business models. Every time Google rolled out a major algorithm update — Panda, Penguin, Hummingbird, Helpful Content — the same panic ensued. Marketers declared that search was finished. I pushed back each time with: “SEO isn’t dead. It’s just evolving.”

This time, however, the underlying shift is fundamentally different from anything we’ve seen over the past 25 years.

In prior cycles, the rules changed, but the referee stayed the same. Google updated its algorithms, penalized black-hat tactics and forced brands to create better experiences. Through it all, Mountain View remained the undisputed gatekeeper of the internet.

Google isn’t just updating the rules this time. It is losing its monopoly over human intent.

Discovery is decentralizing. Consumers no longer instinctively open a browser window, navigate to a search bar and wade through ten blue links buried beneath four sponsored ads. Instead, discovery happens natively where users live, via ambient operating systems, vertical AI engines and conversational interfaces.

Take my own household as a real-world case study:

I genuinely can’t remember anyone in my family running a standard Google search.

This behavioral pivot is driving massive market shifts. Tech market corrections and capital reallocations, such as Alphabet shedding hundreds of billions in market cap during major competitive platform announcements, are not anomalies. They are a lagging indicator of a structural reality: Google’s absolute control over the web’s front door has permanently fractured.

As user behavior shifts from rigid keywords (“best running shoes flat feet”) to complex, conversational prompts (“Compare the top stability running shoes for wide, flat feet under $200 with solid arch support for marathon prep”), standard keyword density and thin programmatic landing pages fail completely.

Enter Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), also referred to as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).

If your marketing leadership is still treating AEO as a minor technical checklist item — uploading an llms.txt file, structuring basic JSON-LD schema and tweaking H2s to question formats — you are missing the forest for the trees.

Winning citation share inside modern language models demands an integrated on-page and off-page architecture built around four core pillars:

Large language models prioritize information efficiency. Models bypass content that regurgitates commodity definitions. Winning content provides primary data, original research, proprietary case studies and clear, structured answers that an engine can cleanly ingest and quote without wading through filler.

LLMs operate on probabilistic associative networks and massive training corpora. If authoritative industry publications, trade journals and top-tier editorial outlets do not regularly cite your brand in direct association with your specific vertical, the model won’t know you exist. Instead, it will synthesize and recommend your competitors.

Answer engines heavily weigh verified public consensus. Unstructured discussions across Reddit, niche communities, review aggregators and professional directories serve as foundational data for conversational engines. Unmonitored reputation issues or a total absence from peer-to-peer discourse directly leads to exclusion from AI recommendations.

AEO requires managing how your brand is perceived across multiple distinct engines, such as Perplexity, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI. Because these systems ingest public social platforms to gauge real-time cultural relevance and expertise, your organic social footprint and executive thought leadership now directly fuel your search visibility.

SEO is not dead, but gone are the days of optimizing exclusively for a single search engine algorithm.

Sustainable organic visibility requires understanding how multi-modal models ingest, evaluate, synthesize and attribute authoritative sources across the entire open web. For entrepreneurs and executives planning growth initiatives, ensuring your business is cited, trusted and surfaced by generative answer engines is no longer an experimental line item. It is foundational to enterprise value.

#5484. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5482. We lead MIT’s FutureTech program on the economics of AI: Don’t ask if AI can do the job, ask how much it costs

Damian Saccocio is Strategic Partnerships Coordinator at MIT FutureTech and an adjunct Professor of Technology Strategy at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business. Neil Thompson is Director of MIT FutureTech and a principal research scientist at MIT CSAIL and the MIT Initiative on the Digital Economy.

Every week seems to bring a major new advance in AI’s ability to do heretofore human-only work, heightening concerns of large-scale and rapid job loss for knowledge workers. Our research at MIT FutureTech suggests the reality is likely to be much more nuanced, with cost, not just capabilities, playing a major role.

Our study of computer vision made this case first. Most research on “AI exposure” measures which tasks AI could potentially perform, focusing on where the technology might develop. That’s a far cry from what we studied: whether firms would actually choose to automate those tasks once they had to pay to build, deploy and maintain the AI system. Across about 1,000 vision tasks in roughly 800 U.S. occupations, only 23% of the wages paid for those tasks were worth automating at the costs of the time.

The reason is fixed cost. A system costs about the same to build whether it replaces an hour of one worker’s day or the shifts of a hundred workers. Consider a bakery that wants to use computer vision to check for ingredient spoilage. If you are the Wonder Bread factory, producing 70+ million loaves of bread per year, it might make sense to automate this task. If you are a corner bakery, any reasonable amount of upfront fixed costs will quickly eclipse your labor savings. So the factory automates and the bakery keeps its bakers.

Generative AI, the AI powering large language models, is different. A general-purpose model sold by the token is far cheaper to start using than a custom vision system, so the fixed-cost barrier is lower. Our newer research asks how good that work is. Experienced workers graded AI output on more than 6,000 text-based tasks from the Labor Department’s occupational database, over 60,000 evaluations in all. The most capable models produced work usable as-is about two-thirds of the time.

That is impressive, but a two-thirds success rate can hide two different realities: AI may handle some tasks well every time and others poorly, or succeed at a given task only some of the time. Either way, firms must work out where AI can be trusted, and pay people to review its work or do the rest. That is part of the real cost of AI. Moving from “usually right” to “reliably right” is often the most expensive step. For most tasks, AI is a collaborator rather than a replacement. It is also improving like a rising tide, steadily and across most tasks at once, not in sudden waves that sweep away one occupation overnight.

Of course, even gradual automation changes what work is worth. But here again the impact is nuanced, because the wage effect depends on which part of a job is automated. For example, when GPS became readily accessible on simple mobile devices, the expertise required of taxi drivers fell, and so did their wages. Conversely, when software took over routine checking from proofreaders, the remaining work demanded more expertise, and wages rose. The same technology can raise pay in one occupation and lower it in another.

The lesson for all is to look past AI exposure. Capabilities matter, but business leaders in particular should judge AI by its full cost per task, including review and correction, not by demos. Policymakers should track AI’s cost and reliability, not just its capabilities. And workers and employers should ask which part of a job AI takes, because that decides whether the remaining work is worth more or less.

Firms will hand work to AI when it is cheaper than a person, not when a demo says it can do the job. That point will arrive task by task and firm by firm, and which tasks go first will decide whose pay rises and whose falls. So the question to ask is not whether AI can do the job. It is what it costs.

#5481. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5480. Continental is considering closing its South African tire factory, risking about 950 jobs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The company cited underused capacity and low-cost imports; operations in Gqeberha could stop by early 2027 if no alternative emerges

Continental is considering ending tire production at its plant in Gqeberha, South Africa, a move that could affect approximately 950 employees, the company said on Friday.

Continental has started a consultation process under Section 189A of South Africa's Labour Relations Act to explore alternatives and discuss ways to reduce the impact on workers. If the process identifies no viable alternative, operations at the site could be discontinued by early 2027, the company said.

Continental said the plant's production capacity has been underused for several years despite turnaround efforts. The company stated that the intensifying price competition from low-cost imports has placed significant pressure on the African tire market. It added that costlier energy, disrupted supply chains and shaky infrastructure have driven up manufacturing costs and complicated forward planning.

The company said South Africa and the wider African continent remain important markets. Its local sales organization will keep serving customers in South Africa and across the region out of Gqeberha, and its BestDrive retail network will not be affected by any changes to production.

The plant has made tires in Gqeberha since 1947. Production of Continental-branded tires began there in 1985, supplying automakers operating in South Africa and the African replacement market, the company said.

A Continental closure would follow other plant shutdowns in South Africa's auto industry, according to Bloomberg. Manufacturers there have had difficulty holding their own against a growing wave of shipments from China and India. Goodyear Tire & Rubber shut down its tire manufacturing site in South Africa in 2025, ending a run of 78 years.

#5479. I Never Saw My Team’s Daily Work as Content. It Turned Out to Be a Powerful Marketing Tool.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The everyday work you take for granted could be the most compelling story your business has to tell.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, I thought I knew what separated my moving company from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always said moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

And I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the company. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

During the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”

Every day, we dealt with closing delays, low bridges, furniture that wouldn’t fit, last-minute additions and customers navigating one of the most stressful days of their lives. To me, that was second nature. To him, it was a story, and he told me we needed to film it.

That eventually became an unscripted docuseries about our company, but it also changed how I thought about growing a business. Until then, we had relied solely on word of mouth. What I hadn’t realized was that showing people what sets us apart from the competition could become a growth strategy.

When you spend every day doing the same thing, you lose sight of what makes it interesting. I didn’t think twice about the problems we encountered on a move, because solving them was my job. But to an outsider, the process was wild. Parking and loading our truck, for example, fascinated our cameraman. It made me realize that the work my team and I do takes real skill.

That’s something business owners in any industry can overlook. You don’t need a glamorous product or a business built for social media to have a story worth telling. A contractor solving a job site issue, a restaurant prepping for a Saturday night or a bookseller opening their store all have something customers rarely get to see.

Simply put, your best content could already be happening. You just have to recognize and document it.

When we started filming, I had to unlearn some of my business owner instincts. After our second day, my wife paused a piece of footage and asked what I had been thinking in that moment. The truth was, I had been thinking plenty. I just wasn’t saying it.

I was trained to stay calm even when things went off the rails. My wife told me to talk to the camera like I was talking to my best friend. I had to rewire my thinking: Explain the problem. Share what you’re thinking. Admit when you’re frustrated. Just be real.

That taught me the difference between advertising and real storytelling. Business owners spend a lot of time telling customers who they are: We’re trustworthy. We care. We go above and beyond. And so on.

Documenting our work allowed us to show those things instead. Our motto is “We take the stress out of your move,” and now people could see that firsthand: how our crew wraps belongings to protect them from torrential rain, how we responded when a move didn’t go as planned because of an insurance headache and how we treated customers even when we were close to pulling our hair out under high-pressure deadlines. The messy moments showed more about the company than the camera-ready ones.

Other entrepreneurs can learn from this. What do you claim about your business that you could demonstrate instead?

After we finished filming the show, a former customer who worked in the film industry encouraged us to start sharing our story on social media. Creating content consistently has sometimes felt like starting another business, but it also changed how I think about marketing. Traditional advertising usually tries to reach someone around the time they’re ready to buy. Telling a story and building an audience can create a relationship long before that.

That’s especially important in a business like moving. People don’t need movers every month. Someone might discover one of our videos today and not move for another year. But if they keep following the company and seeing our crew at work, we don’t have to introduce ourselves when they’re finally ready for a quote. The audience comes first. The customer can come later.

And we’re starting to see that play out. When we ask new customers how they found us, more and more of them mention our videos. One man contacted us about moving his lemon trees because he’d seen us move palm trees on Instagram. During another move, a customer’s 6-year-old recognized us from our YouTube Shorts. To me, that was proof: People weren’t just remembering our moving company. They were remembering us. They felt like they’d gotten to know the people behind the business, and more importantly, they already trusted us.

Don’t get me wrong: You don’t need to create a docuseries to apply this strategy. I’d start with three questions:

The goal isn’t to capture someone’s attention for the sole purpose of selling something. That’s empty, and it doesn’t build trust. The point is to give viewers, your potential customers, a reason to keep paying attention.

Your competitors can offer similar services. They can lower their prices and make the same claims about why they’re better. What they can’t replicate is your people, your experiences, your perspective and how you do your work.

For years, I thought I knew what separated my moving company from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always said moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

And I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the company. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

During the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”

#5478. The Expedia breach shows why companies must stop holding data they do not need

Raj Ananthanpillai is the founder and CEO of Trua and the author of the recently published book The Trust Crisis: How Big Tech Stole Your Identity—and the New Model That Takes It Back. Trua verifies identity without requiring organizations to retain the underlying documents.

Expedia Group confirmed on Nov. 12 that attackers reached its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider. An extortion group has claimed to possess hundreds of millions of traveler-related records, although the volume and contents of any stolen data remain unverified. The investigation is ongoing. But the incident already points to a larger problem: businesses and their vendors routinely accumulate more personal information than they need to perform the task at hand.

I have a commercial stake in this argument, and I want to be clear about it. My company, Trua, offers an alternative: verifying identity without requiring every organization to retain the underlying documents. But I also have spent years working on credentialing systems and seeing what becomes possible when organizations separate the assurance they need from the sensitive records they do not.

Before Trua, my previous company helped develop technology that ultimately became part of TSA PreCheck and other credential programs. The design question we kept returning to was not how much information we could collect, but what the checkpoint actually needed to know. Enrollment involved verifying government identification and other biographical details, conducting checks against criminal and terrorism databases, and issuing a Known Traveler Number after clearance. At screening, however, the relevant answer was much narrower: was the traveler approved? The lane could rely on credential validation and biometric authentication rather than access to the full background file, Social Security number, or other enrollment records. Those remained with the vetting authority.

That distinction mattered. We did not make the original verification less rigorous; we made the result usable without passing the underlying dossier from system to system. A screening officer needed a trustworthy determination, not a copy of the investigation behind it. The approach supported a faster process while reducing the amount of sensitive information exposed at each point of use.

Much of the private sector still operates in the opposite direction. Companies collect identity documents, payment information, travel histories, and other personal details for a particular transaction, then keep them available long afterward. Copies move into interconnected vendor environments, often with persistent access. When a trusted supplier is compromised, the exposure can extend well beyond the supplier itself—as the Expedia incident illustrates.

The problem often becomes visible only when someone audits what has accumulated. One midsize staffing firm found roughly 180,000 applicant and worker records in its systems. About 35 percent were more than six years old, and more than half related to people who had never been hired or had left years earlier. Files containing Social Security numbers and background reports had been copied to at least four vendors and two client HR systems. No single decision created that liability. It grew with each onboarding form, integration, and decision to keep a record just in case.

Most organizations do not need those permanent copies to make the decisions before them. A travel platform may need to confirm a customer’s identity and payment validity. An employer may need to know whether an applicant holds a required credential or meets screening criteria. Those are questions that can be answered with reliable, purpose-specific confirmations. Retaining every source document is not the same as improving the quality of the answer.

The incentives behind overcollection are understandable, but increasingly costly. Businesses want speed and certainty. Technology vendors often design services around access to raw data. Risk assessments can treat large stores of personal information as an unavoidable feature of doing business rather than a choice to be challenged. And as AI agents begin taking actions on people’s behalf, organizations will need to establish who authorized a transaction and what that agent is permitted to do. Without a better model, that need could become an excuse to create yet more identity databases.

There is another way. Individuals can undergo strong verification and then share only the attributes or status required for a specific purpose. The receiving organization gets a trustworthy, appropriately limited response, potentially subject to expiration or revalidation, rather than a dossier it must protect indefinitely. Selective-disclosure mobile driver’s licenses and other attribute-verification systems show how this can work. It does not eliminate cybersecurity risk, but it reduces the quantity of sensitive information dispersed across corporate and vendor systems.

The exact scope of the Expedia intrusion remains to be established. The broader lesson does not. As long as every business transaction generates another lasting store of personal records, a breach at one trusted provider can create risks for many organizations and the people who rely on them. The durable response is not merely to defend ever-larger databases. It is to collect less, retain less, and share only what a particular decision requires. Businesses should treat unnecessary retention as a liability, insurers should price that liability, and policymakers should give data minimization as much attention as breach response. Otherwise, we will keep reading versions of the same headline.

#5477. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5476. Toyota is recalling more than 314,000 vehicles over aging Takata airbag risk

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The recall covers Toyota and Lexus models from the 2002 through 2017 model years, and dealers will make repairs free of charge

Toyota $TM is recalling more than 314,000 Toyota and Lexus models sold in the U.S., the company said on Nov. 12, citing Takata-made inflators in the front passenger airbag that can rupture and send metal fragments into the cabin.

The inflator propellant can degrade over time in certain temperature and humidity conditions, Toyota said. If the airbag deploys, a ruptured inflator can drive metal fragments through the airbag at high speed, which may injure or kill vehicle occupants.

The recall applies to 314,029 vehicles built for model years 2002 to 2017, according to Fox Business. Toyota reported no ruptures involving the affected inflators and is carrying out the recall as a precaution.

The affected vehicles include 2002-2010 Lexus SC430 convertibles, 2011 Lexus IS250 sedans and convertibles, and 2017 Lexus GX460 SUVs, according to Consumer Reports. The list also has 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla sedans, 2005-2006 Toyota Tundra trucks, 2005-2007 Toyota Sequoia SUVs and 2016-2017 Toyota 4Runner SUVs.

Depending on the model, Toyota said, dealers for both brands will swap out either the front passenger inflator or the entire airbag assembly at no cost to owners.

Owners can enter a vehicle identification number or license plate information at Toyota.com/recall or nhtsa.gov/recalls to see whether a vehicle is involved, Toyota said. Toyota customer support is available at 1-800-331-4331.

Notification letters to owners are scheduled to go out from Toyota between Dec. 28 and Jan. 11, according to Fox Business. Owners can reach out to a dealer to arrange a fix without waiting for the letters to show up.

The recall adds to a string of Takata airbag recalls dating back to 2014, according to Consumer Reports.

#5475. Study: 403 U.S. data centers rival Denmark’s carbon emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

#5474. 3 steps that shrink California's quake insurance gap, and where each falls short

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nearly 90% of California homeowners had no quake coverage in 2018. Three steps from a USGS geophysicist cut the risk but leave the gap open.

Californians tend to treat earthquakes as background, a risk they know about and seldom plan for. Experts don't treat that risk as remote. Over the next 30 years, the Hayward Fault by itself has a 33% chance of producing a large quake, according to U.S. Geological Survey figures reported by BLS. That window matches the term of a standard home mortgage, and a family that buys a house near that fault faces real odds of living through the quake before the loan is paid off. Each household decides on its own whether to insure against that risk, and the sum of those private choices is the state's insurance gap.

Many homeowners who skip coverage expect government help to cover the damage when the quake comes. The scale of a bad quake makes that a weak plan. Estimates of insured and uninsured damages from a magnitude 6.9 quake on the Hayward Fault run as high as $210‒$235 billion, according to BLS. At the high end of that range, a great many households across the region would need help at the same moment. For an uninsured homeowner, the useful question is what the family can do before the ground moves to make the loss smaller and the days after it survivable.

NPR reported on steps that Ken Hudnut, a geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey, says Californians should take to build earthquake resilience, from the strength of a home's foundation to the food and water in its cupboards. The need for those steps was plain in 2018, when nearly 90% of California homeowners had no quake coverage and federal disaster aid to an individual was capped at about $33,000. That cap is far below what a major quake can destroy, so most of an uninsured family's loss would stay with the family. "There's a lot you need to do to insure resilience for yourself, your family, your home, your workplace," Hudnut said. A policy is only one piece of that work, and the rest of it falls to the household.

Preparing a home and buying quake coverage work together, even though many uninsured homeowners treat preparation as a substitute for a policy. Damage to buildings alone is a large bill. Estimates for a magnitude 6.9 quake on the Hayward Fault vary widely, and even the lowest puts building-related losses at $23 billion, according to BLS. Some preparation also lowers the cost of coverage, since insurers price policies around a structure’s strength.

Homeowners who skip coverage often assume a major quake will strike on some other fault. U.S. Geological Survey figures give the San Andreas Fault a 22% chance of a major rupture within 30 years, lower than the Hayward Fault’s, according to BLS. Yet a magnitude 7.2 quake on the San Andreas would bring moderate to heavy shaking to places that pay 17.0% of Bay Area wages, BLS estimates. Lower odds don’t mean a smaller loss.

Preparation can make a quake less costly, but it doesn’t replace a policy.

A foundation retrofit lets an owner change how much a quake can take from the house itself. Well-designed, well-built buildings take only negligible damage at intensity VII on the Modified Mercalli scale, according to BLS, and construction quality is one of the few things an owner can improve ahead of time. Hudnut counts a foundation check among his key steps. In 2018, a completed upgrade could also earn up to 20% off California Earthquake Authority coverage, according to NPR, but only for owners who buy a policy. For the uninsured majority, the payoff is a sturdier house, not a smaller premium.

Public money for retrofits goes mainly to owners whom a city has already ordered to act. A grant for apartment buildings is open only to owners who have received a city notice and order to retrofit, the California Residential Mitigation Program reports, and it runs in 14 California cities with mandatory ordinances. “Buildings that qualify for this grant are already required by law to retrofit under their city’s ordinance,” said Janiele Maffei, chief mitigation officer at the California Earthquake Authority.

Even an owner who qualifies still pays part of the bill. Qualifying owners get 70% of their construction costs paid, up to $4,260 per unit, according to the program, and cover the rest themselves.

A strengthened foundation limits the damage to a house, but most owners pay for it themselves, and it leaves the insurance gap open.

The first hardship after a major quake is getting through days without power, running water or open stores, and it arrives long before any insurance claim or aid check is settled. Hudnut advises Californians to keep emergency packs stocked with food and water for several days so they can survive outages and displacement, according to NPR. Federal health officials also measure readiness in days, and the CDC advises keeping earthquake supplies for at least three days. A stocked kit helps a family on the first night, well before any payout could, and a household with no policy can still rely on it.

A useful quake kit holds more than food and water. The CDC recommends adding sturdy shoes, heavy gloves, a fire extinguisher and a whistle to a home kit, so people can walk over broken glass, put out a small fire and signal for help. Checking a kit means checking that gear as well as the dates on the food.

The three-day standard is a floor, and households need to plan past it. The CDC also calls for a supply kit in the car, because supplies are useful only if they go with the family. A second kit means the household has supplies wherever it ends up.

With a full kit, a family can get through the first few days after a quake, but it needs a plan of its own for the weeks that follow.

#5473. Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first 100-day agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt

While it’s the responsibility of the Department of the Treasury to finance the interest on the U.S.’s $40 trillion national debt, it is members of both parties in Congress who have added to Uncle Sam’s borrowing.With the Democrats winning a wave of seats in the midterm elections, everyone from Wall Street analysts to CEOs of America’s largest companies are wondering what a more divided government will mean.Budget watchdogs are doing the same, and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) has put a number on how much the Democrats’ plan for their first 100 days will cost.

The Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with slim majorities in both chambers, and they have been clear about what they want to achieve in their first three months with more power. Hakeem Jeffries, nominated by Democrats to be the Speaker of the House of Representatives, wrote in November that the first 100-day agenda comprises “reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs, and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran.”

Some factors come with obvious budget implications: De-escalating the war in the Middle East would save money, while ending Trump tariffs would axe a revenue stream that generated $287 billion in customs duties, taxes, and fees in 2025 per the Richmond Fed—up 192% on the prior year.

The CRFB estimates that, in total, the “First 100 Days” policies would cost $4.1 trillion through 2037. Without offsets (spending cuts or revenue increases used to balance new policies), $4.9 trillion would be added to the debt burden over the next decade, including interest costs.

But the factor analysts—and budget hawks—really care about is the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio. This describes the level of borrowing a nation has relative to its economic growth, and therefore its ability to service that borrowing. At the moment, it stands at around 121%, per the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

Economists suggest that if this balance were to tip further, then U.S. lenders may begin demanding higher premiums to offset the risk associated with the borrowing—sparking a bond crisis.

The House Democrats’ policies would increase the debt-to-GDP ratio to 135% by 2037 without offsets, versus 125% of GDP under an adjusted CBO baseline, the CRFB added.

The budget watchdog does offer some alternatives for how revenue to offset these proposals could be generated, though the reforms are unlikely to be popular with voters.

“Repealing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s (OBBBA) tax cuts for high earners would generate about $2 trillion of savings—enough to offset an agenda scaled back by half,” the budget watchdog wrote.

“Repealing all of the tax cuts and spending increases in OBBBA—including its low-income and middle-class tax cuts—would generate about $7 trillion. That would be enough to pay for the First 100 Days agenda 1.7 times over.”

The budget committee broke down each aspect of the proposals by line.

Starting first with the policies that could save money, the CRFB pointed to Iran. It noted that while ending the conflict would not immediately reduce deficits, it would likely avoid increases in military and defense spending. Continuing the war in Iran, the committee writes, costs approximately $30 billion a year and could be avoided.

Regarding policy costs for 2027-2037, removing Trump’s tariffs leaves the largest budget hole. This represents $1.8 trillion in total, from repealing Section 301 tariffs (costing $955 billion alone) and Section 232 tariffs ($780 billion) to undoing Section 338 tariffs on certain Canadian goods ($35 billion).

Reversing the OBBBA health provisions would cost $1.6 trillion by 2037, the committee adds, including $600 billion to cancel provider tax and state-directed payment limits, as well as $485 billion to remove Medicaid work requirements. Reversing SNAP provisions would cost $250 billion over the next 10 years.

Increasing the deficit would also mean larger interest payments on the debt, the CRFB added—some $840 billion over the next 10 years.

#5472. I Used to Counteroffer My Best Employees With More Money. Now I Rely on These 3 Strategies.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Raises and equity can delay a top performer’s exit, but smarter compensation structures can keep them for the long haul.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

Given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or company equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

I am not suggesting that it is wrong to counteroffer someone’s resignation with money. However, it’s reactive and arbitrary. Unless you have put a cap on how high you are willing to go, your negotiations will begin to feel like a moving target that’s out of your control. Again, you may end up delaying someone’s departure, but you won’t keep them forever unless you put more proactive measures in place.

Some positions in your company drive enterprise value and some don’t. McKinsey and Company suggested in an older article that these will probably make up about 5% of your workforce — and contribute 800% more than others across your organization.

Over the years, I’ve found that I could typically name fewer than 10 roles that would materially impact my business if they remained vacant for an extended period. My recommendation is to name those roles and then create retention plans for each of them.

What are some focused plan ideas? Deferred compensation structures allow team members to grow their money tax-free as long as they stay with your organization. That way, you won’t inflate your overall payroll and can concentrate your resources where they matter most. This type of long-term incentive can be tangibly meaningful because it’s tied to tenure and not merely performance. Since it’s only applicable to a small group of high-value employees, you aren’t raising your compensation across your organization, either.

I once considered using equity as a major retention lever. Why not? It felt right and seemed to be a no-brainer way to get people to stick around and contribute to our company’s growth. Yet when I mapped out the risks and rewards, I realized that giving away equity has massive long-term costs.

Here’s the issue: equity permanently dilutes your ability to use equity in other ways later. For example, you can’t bargain with equity with potential investors if a chunk of it has been given to your employees. Going the equity route also complicates your organizational governance, which can make your financial picture blurry.

Rather than offering equity to someone who wants to leave, explore non-equity alternatives. Treat equity as a last resort that you’ll only consider if you think it will bring out an employee’s long-term ownership behavior. And be open to talking about this with a professional who has helped other businesses design executive benefit and compensation structures that retain key people while protecting tax exposure and equity. Looking for a resource to get your feet wet? Colin Steinberg, a partner at Institutional Architects, frequently shares advice on executive planning and related topics.

There are many business-friendlier alternatives to simply handing an employee who’s about to leave more money or equity. As mentioned before, you might provide deferred compensation, a way to delay income that benefits both you and the team member.

You might also look into supplemental executive retirement plans. Chances are strong that you already offer retirement benefits. Could you offer additional ones directly tied to both tenure and performance? Supplemental executive retirement plans help C-suite employees see meaningful future value in putting down roots, which SmartAsset explains can help trim churn among your highest-paid performers.

When structured appropriately, these types of retention strategies avoid immediate financial strain on your balance sheet. They also allow you to turn retention tools into ways to improve your tax efficiency, reduce volatile compensation models and retain control over your equity.

I firmly believe that founders who lose their most valuable people (but are otherwise building solid, fair companies) don’t have a problem with their retention. They have a problem with the way they’ve structured their long-term compensation packages for their most impactful roles. If you want to get real leverage as an employer, you need to develop smarter systems that incentivize your key players without losing your ground.

Like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

Given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or company equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

#5471. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:38 am

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

ARK Invest bought about $90.8 million of Anthropic stock across six of its funds on Thursday, the day the AI company began trading on the Nasdaq $NDAQ, according to CNBC. ARK, founded and run by CEO Cathie Wood, had a pre-IPO position in Anthropic through its ARK Venture Fund.

The firm bought roughly 935,000 shares of Anthropic stock in total, according to CoinDesk. ARK Innovation ETF accounted for 556,777 of those shares, CoinDesk said, citing an emailed trading update from the firm.

Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, selling 980 million shares of Class A common stock. The offering totals $81 billion, topping the $75 billion SpaceX collected in its IPO before its underwriters exercised their overallotment option.

Of the shares sold, Anthropic is selling 956,351,354 and certain selling stockholders are selling 23,648,646. Anthropic receives no proceeds from the selling stockholders' portion. #5469. Bitcoin Price, Gold and Oil Fall: Should the US Repeat Its $2.2T 2020 Rescue?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

Almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

October’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also said a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

The risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets quickly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

The Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

President Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

The current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

The Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

The Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

At the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

But the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

#5468. Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy

Good morning. Intuit is unwinding its biggest acquisition while betting AI can help it win customers without owning the marketing platform it once viewed as central to that effort.

The QuickBooks and TurboTax parent announced Thursday it plans to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing automation platform, to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to approval, with proceeds earmarked for fiscal 2027 share repurchases. Intuit paid approximately $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021. Mailchimp’s quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313 million.

Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit (No. 231 on the Fortune 500) said on the earnings call that Intuit still wants to help businesses manage lead-to-cash needs, but believes it can do so more effectively by building AI-powered capabilities into QuickBooks rather than owning Mailchimp.

The divestiture adds another dimension to what CFO Sandeep Aujla has called Intuit’s “reset to reaccelerate” strategy launched in August: accepting some near-term pressure on revenue per customer to rebuild customer acquisition. The strategy includes lower upfront revenue per TurboTax customer as Intuit seeks faster customer growth.

The latest results offered evidence of operating momentum. For the fiscal first quarter ended Oct. 31, revenue rose 12% to $4.35 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 56% to $2.91. Both exceeded analyst expectations.

In my conversation with Aujla, he pointed to mid-market revenue growth of 41% and customer growth of 30% as evidence that Intuit’s major growth initiatives are gaining traction. He also emphasized management’s commitment to delivering on its promises.

But the outlook exposed pressure at Credit Karma from tighter financing conditions and changing consumer behavior.

Intuit now forecasts fiscal 2027 revenue of $23.08 billion to $23.37 billion, lowering its outlook to reflect slower expected growth at Credit Karma amid tighter lending conditions and changing consumer behavior. It maintained its adjusted earnings forecast of $22.88 to $23.12 a share. Neither forecast includes the pending Mailchimp sale. The stock was down about 13% in after-hours trading.

Aujla said conditions have shifted since Intuit set its guidance in August, when the debate centered on whether the Federal Reserve would hold interest rates steady or lower them. He described the environment now as one of tightening, with higher rates slowing consumer demand in the categories Credit Karma serves. Lending partners are still expanding, he said, but at a slower pace.

AI reshapes Credit Karma’s customer acquisition

At the same time, changes in how consumers seek financial information are affecting Credit Karma.

“The evolution of consumer behavior is impacting us faster than what we had anticipated,” Aujla told me.

Historically, only about 1% of Credit Karma’s customers came through search engines, he said. Now, consumers increasingly turn to AI for initial answers before visiting Credit Karma, creating a new customer acquisition challenge.

“More customers are going to AI to get the first answer,” he said.

Intuit plans to apply lessons from QuickBooks and TurboTax to improve Credit Karma’s visibility in AI-generated responses, Aujla said. AI is thus both a product opportunity and a customer acquisition challenge.

Regarding the market’s reaction, Aujla said that during major technological shifts, whether cloud computing, mobile or now AI, “it’s just human nature to overreact to the uncertainty and the pendulum swings.” He sees the reaction as an overcorrection, with investors questioning whether companies can successfully navigate the changes.

“What we are underwriting is, in our 40-plus years of history, we’ve been able to evolve and continue to come out of every change in the marketplace,” he said.

Have a good weekend. Sheryl EstradaSheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

#5467. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.
